readmePreview: Fast, unopinionated, minimalist web framework for Node.js.

overview.summary: Express 5.2.1 is the minimalist Node.js HTTP framework, and this repository holds only its core: ~5,500 lines across six files in `lib/` that layer settings management, request/response sugar, and a template-resolution system on top of Node's `http` primitives. What is distinctive about the v5 line is how much has been pushed out of the tree — routing lives entirely in the external `router` package, body parsing in `body-parser`, static serving in `serve-static` — so this repo is mostly a prototype-mixin façade plus a large behavioural test suite (70 unit files, 18 acceptance files that boot the `examples/` apps). It targets Node >= 18 and ships to npm as a library; there is no build step, no bundler, and no storage layer. The audience is every Node web developer, and the maintenance posture is visibly conservative: pinned SHA GitHub Actions, OpenSSF Scorecard, CodeQL, dependabot with major-version updates ignored.

system_map.summary: A single npm entrypoint (`index.js` → `lib/express.js`) exposes a factory, `createApplication()`, that returns a callable function decorated with the application prototype and EventEmitter. Five runtime modules split responsibility: `application.js` (settings, dispatch, mounting, rendering), `request.js` and `response.js` (prototypes grafted onto `http.IncomingMessage`/`http.ServerResponse`), `view.js` (template lookup), and `utils.js` (compilers for etag/query/trust). The runtime boundary is deliberately thin — routing, body parsing and static file serving are re-exported from sibling npm packages rather than implemented here. There is no persistent storage; all state is per-app in-memory objects. Distribution is npm-only, driven by a GitHub release event.

claims.claim: `index.js` is a three-line re-export of `lib/express.js`, and `package.json` restricts the published tarball to `LICENSE`, `Readme.md`, `index.js` and `lib/` — so `test/` and `examples/` never ship.

`createApplication()` builds `app` as a closure that forwards to `app.handle(req, res, next)`, then uses `merge-descriptors` to mixin `EventEmitter.prototype` and the `application` proto (both with `redefine=false`), and finally calls `app.init()`.

Per-app request/response prototypes are created with `Object.create(req, { app: {...value: app} })`, which is why every `req`/`res` getter can reach `this.app.get('trust proxy fn')` without a closure.

Routing is not implemented in this repo: `lib/express.js` requires the external `router` package and re-exports `Router` and `Router.Route`; `app.router` is a lazy getter that instantiates `new Router({ caseSensitive, strict })` on first access.
Body parsing is a pure re-export — `express.json`, `express.raw`, `express.text`, `express.urlencoded` all point straight at `body-parser`, and `express.static` at `serve-static`.

All per-app state lives in three null-prototype objects created in `app.init()` — `this.cache` (compiled views), `this.engines` (extension→renderer), `this.settings` — plus `this.locals`; there is no database or persistence layer anywhere in `lib/`.

`app.handle()` is the single dispatch boundary: it builds a `finalhandler` terminator, sets `X-Powered-By`, wires the `req.res`/`res.req` circular refs, swaps both prototypes with `Object.setPrototypeOf`, and delegates to `this.router.handle`.

The external integration surface is 28 runtime dependencies, of which the load-bearing ones are `proxy-addr` (trust proxy), `qs`/`node:querystring` (query), `send`+`serve-static` (file IO), `etag`+`fresh` (conditional GET), `cookie`+`cookie-signature`, and `finalhandler`.

There is no build step. The npm scripts are `lint` (eslint), `test` (mocha over `test/` and `test/acceptance/` with `--check-leaks`), `test-ci` (nyc → lcovonly), `test-cov` (nyc → html) and `test-tap`.
CI runs a 2-OS × 9-Node matrix (ubuntu/windows × Node 18–26) in `ci.yml`, with a separate `legacy.yml` still exercising Node 16 and 17 despite `engines.node` declaring `>= 18`.

Deployment is npm publish triggered by GitHub release `published`; the workflow derives the dist-tag from `package.json` version rather than the release branch (`next` for prereleases, `latest` for the newest major, `latest-<major>` for maintenance lines).

Supply-chain hardening is explicit: `.npmrc` disables lockfiles, enforces a 7-day minimum release age, sets `ignore-scripts=true` and `allow-git=none`; every Action in CI is pinned to a full commit SHA.

feature_catalog.summary: The user-facing surface is three prototypes plus a factory. `app` provides configuration (`set`/`get`/`enable`/`disable`/`enabled`/`disabled`), composition (`use`, `route`, `param`, `all`, one method per `http.METHODS` entry), templating (`engine`, `render`) and lifecycle (`listen`, `path`). `res` provides ~24 response helpers built around `res.send`. `req` provides content negotiation and a set of lazily-computed getters derived from headers and the trust-proxy setting. The `examples/` tree doubles as documentation for 26 usage patterns and as the fixture set for acceptance tests.

claims.claim: HTTP verb methods are generated dynamically: `methods.forEach` iterates `require('node:http').METHODS` lowercased and defines `app[method]`, with `app.get(name)` special-cased to read a setting when called with exactly one argument.
`app.all(path, ...fns)` registers the same handlers against every method in the generated `methods` list rather than using a wildcard.

`app.set()` has four magic settings that compile a companion function: `etag`→`etag fn`, `query parser`→`query parser fn`, `trust proxy`→`trust proxy fn`; each compiler throws `TypeError` on unknown string values.

Defaults set at boot: `x-powered-by` enabled, `etag` = `weak`, `query parser` = `simple` (node querystring), `subdomain offset` = 2, `trust proxy` = false, `jsonp callback name` = `callback`, `views` = `resolve('views')`, and `view cache` auto-enabled when `NODE_ENV === 'production'`.

`app.use()` detects a mounted sub-app by duck-typing `fn.handle && fn.set`, wraps it in a `mounted_app` middleware that restores the parent's `req`/`res` prototypes on the way out, sets `mountpath`/`parent`, and emits `'mount'`.

The `'mount'` listener installed in `defaultConfiguration` makes a child app prototype-inherit the parent's `request`, `response`, `engines` and `settings`, and drops its own default `trust proxy` so the parent's wins.

`res.send` is the funnel for almost every response: it type-switches on the body, sets Content-Type, computes Content-Length (skipped when `Transfer-Encoding` is present), generates an ETag, downgrades to 304 when `req.fresh`, strips headers for 204/304/205, and skips the body for HEAD.

`res.json` and `res.jsonp` share a `stringify()` helper honouring the `json replacer`, `json spaces` and `json escape` settings, where `json escape` rewrites `<`, `>`, `&` to `\u003c`/`\u003e`/`\u0026` to defeat HTML sniffing.

`res.sendFile(path, opts, cb)` requires an absolute path or an explicit `opts.root`, `encodeURI`s the path, wires `opts.etag` from the app setting, and pipes a `send` stream through the local `sendfile()` state machine; `EISDIR` falls through to `next()`.

`res.download()` layers `Content-Disposition` (via `content-disposition`) on top of `res.sendFile`, explicitly dropping any user-supplied `content-disposition` header and resolving the path when no `root` is given.
`res.format(obj)` negotiates on the object's keys via `req.accepts`, always sets `Vary: Accept`, falls back to an optional `default` key, and otherwise calls `next(createError(406, { types }))`.

`res.redirect` is itself implemented on top of `res.format`, emitting a plain-text or escaped-HTML body for the target, and uses `depd` deprecation warnings for missing/non-string URLs and non-numeric statuses.

data_flow.summary: Data enters as a raw Node `IncomingMessage`, is re-prototyped in `app.handle` so that Express getters become available, then flows through the external router's middleware stack where `body-parser` populates `req.body` and the router populates `req.params`, `req.baseUrl` and `req.next`. Derived request values are computed lazily and are never cached — every read of `req.query`, `req.ip` or `req.host` re-runs its parser against the raw headers, gated by the compiled `trust proxy fn`. Output converges on `res.send`, which is where Content-Type, Content-Length, ETag and freshness negotiation are decided before `res.end`. Template rendering is a side channel: `res.render` → `app.render` → `View#render` produces a string that is then fed back into `res.send`. Anything that escapes the stack terminates in `finalhandler`.

claims.claim: The input boundary is `app.handle(req, res, callback)`, which mutates the incoming Node objects in place via `Object.setPrototypeOf(req, this.request)` / `(res, this.response)` — Express never wraps or copies the request.
`res.locals` is lazily initialised to `Object.create(null)` on each dispatch only if absent, so a sub-app mount reuses the parent's locals object rather than resetting it.

`req.query` is recomputed on every property read: it fetches `query parser fn` from app settings, extracts the raw string with `parseurl`, and returns `Object.create(null)` when parsing is disabled (`query parser` set to `false`).

The `extended` query parser routes through `qs.parse(str, { allowPrototypes: true })`, while the default `simple` parser is `node:querystring.parse` — two materially different object shapes behind one setting.

All proxy-derived values funnel through one compiled predicate: `compileTrust` turns `true`, a hop count, a comma-separated string, an array or a function into `trust(addr, index)`, consumed identically by `req.protocol`, `req.ip`, `req.ips` and `req.host`.
`req.protocol` and `req.host` both defensively split their `X-Forwarded-*` header on the first comma, taking only the left-most value.
`req.ips` reverses `proxyaddr.all()` and pops the socket address, so the returned array is farthest-to-closest and excludes the direct peer.
On the way out, `res.set('Content-Type', ...)` always runs the value through `mime.contentType()` to append a charset, and throws `TypeError` if an array is supplied for Content-Type.

ETag generation is a two-step: `compileETag` picks `wetag`/`etag` from `lib/utils.js`, `res.send` calls it only when no ETag header is already present and a length was computed, and the buffer conversion is skipped for chunks under 1000 bytes when no ETag is needed.

Render data is merged in a fixed precedence — `app.locals`, then `res.locals` (passed as `opts._locals`), then the caller's options — with `cache` defaulting to the `view cache` setting when not explicitly provided.
Compiled views are memoised by name in `app.cache` only when `renderOptions.cache` is truthy, which is why development mode re-stats the filesystem on every render.
`View#render` normalises synchronous engine callbacks by copying `arguments` and deferring through `process.nextTick`, guaranteeing the caller always sees an async callback.

behavior_traces.summary: Four flows carry essentially all of Express's behaviour: application construction, request dispatch, response emission, and view rendering. Each is short and traceable by name — the framework is only three or four stack frames deep before control reaches an external package. The traces below name functions in call order as they appear in `lib/`.

claims.claim: STARTUP: `require('express')` → `index.js` → `lib/express.js` → user calls `createApplication()` → `mixin(app, EventEmitter.prototype)` → `mixin(app, proto)` → `Object.create(req/res)` → `app.init()` → `app.defaultConfiguration()` → settings seeded and the `'mount'` listener attached → `Object.defineProperty(this, 'router', getter)` installs the lazy router.

STARTUP (server): `app.listen(...)` → `http.createServer(this)` → if the last arg is a function it is wrapped with `once()` and registered on the server's `'error'` event → `server.listen.apply(server, args)`; the returned value is the `http.Server`, not the app.
ROUTE REGISTRATION: `app.get('/x', fn)` → generated method sees `arguments.length > 1` → `this.route(path)` → `this.router.route(path)` (first access instantiates `new Router`) → `route.get(fn)`.

DISPATCH: socket → `app(req, res)` closure → `app.handle` → `finalhandler(...)` built → `res.setHeader('X-Powered-By')` → `req.res`/`res.req` cross-links → both prototypes swapped → `res.locals` ensured → `this.router.handle(req, res, done)` hands off to the external router package.

PRIMARY ACTION (`res.send('hi')`): typeof-string branch sets charset via `setCharset` or `this.type('html')` → `app.get('etag fn')` → length computed and `Content-Length` set unless `Transfer-Encoding` present → `etagFn(chunk, encoding)` → `this.set('ETag')` → `if (req.fresh) this.status(304)` → header stripping for 204/304/205 → `this.end(chunk, encoding)` (or bare `end()` for HEAD).

JSON PATH: `res.json(obj)` → reads `json escape`/`json replacer`/`json spaces` → `stringify()` → sets `Content-Type: application/json` only if unset → delegates to `res.send(body)`, which then re-enters the string branch and applies the charset.

JSONP PATH: `res.jsonp` → `stringify()` → reads the callback from `req.query[app.get('jsonp callback name')]` → takes `callback[0]` if an array → strips everything outside `[^\[\]\w$.]` → sets `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff` and `text/javascript` → escapes U+2028/U+2029 → wraps in the `/**/ typeof cb === 'function' && cb(...)` Rosetta-Flash mitigation → `res.send`.

RENDER PATH: `res.render(view, opts)` → `opts._locals = res.locals` → default callback `(err, str) => err ? req.next(err) : self.send(str)` → `app.render(name, opts, done)` → locals merged → cache consulted → `new View(name, { defaultEngine, root, engines })` → `view.lookup()` → `View#resolve` → `tryStat` → `tryRender(view, opts, done)` → `View#render` → engine → `process.nextTick` → `res.send(html)`.

ENGINE RESOLUTION: inside the `View` constructor, if `opts.engines[this.ext]` is missing, Express computes `mod = this.ext.slice(1)` and performs a dynamic `require(mod).__express`, throwing `Module "x" does not provide a view engine.` when that export is not a function.
VIEW LOOKUP fallback: `View#resolve` first tries `<dir>/<file>` and, failing that, `<dir>/<basename>/index<ext>` — both via synchronous `fs.statSync` wrapped in `tryStat`.

FILE TRANSFER: `res.sendFile` → argument validation (throws on missing/non-string path, and on a relative path with no `root`) → `encodeURI(path)` → `opts.etag = app.enabled('etag')` → `send(req, pathname, opts)` → `sendfile(res, file, opts, cb)` → listeners registered → `file.pipe(res)`; the `onfinish` handler uses `setImmediate` to distinguish a completed stream from an aborted one.

DOWNLOAD: `res.download` → argument shuffling for the (filename|options|callback) overloads → `Content-Disposition` built from `basename(name || path)` → caller headers copied except `content-disposition` → `opts = Object.create(opts)` so user options stay on the prototype → `resolve(path)` when no `root` → `this.sendFile(fullPath, opts, done)`.

testing_signals.summary: Testing is mocha + supertest with `after` for multi-assertion coordination, and it is unusually thorough for a codebase this size: 70 unit files under `test/` plus 18 acceptance files under `test/acceptance/`, totalling ~15,400 lines against ~5,500 lines of `lib/`. Unit files are named one-per-API (`res.send.js`, `req.host.js`, `app.param.js`), which makes the mapping from source method to test file mechanical. Acceptance tests do not use fixtures — they `require('../../examples/<name>')` and drive the real example apps, so `examples/` is effectively production test surface. Coverage runs through nyc in CI across the whole matrix, is merged with lcov and shipped to Coveralls.

claims.claim: The runner is mocha with `--require test/support/env --check-leaks`, covering both `test/` and `test/acceptance/`; `--check-leaks` means any accidental global assignment fails the suite.
`test/support/env.js` forces `NODE_ENV=test` (which suppresses `logerror` output and keeps `view cache` disabled) and sets `NO_DEPRECATION=body-parser,express` to silence `depd` warnings.
HTTP assertions run through `supertest` against the app function directly, without binding a port — e.g. `request(app).get('/').expect(200, done)`.

`test/support/utils.js` provides the shared assertion vocabulary: `shouldHaveBody`, `shouldHaveHeader`, `shouldNotHaveBody`, `shouldNotHaveHeader`, `shouldSkipQuery` — with body comparison done on hex-encoded buffers.
`test/support/tmpl.js` is a hand-rolled `$var.path` template engine used as the canonical view-engine double, avoiding a real engine dependency in most view tests.

The largest test files track the riskiest code: `app.router.js` (1217 lines), `res.sendFile.js` (913), `express.urlencoded.js` (828), `express.static.js` (815), `express.json.js` (755), `Router.js` (636), `res.send.js` (635).

Path-traversal behaviour is explicitly covered: `express.static.js` asserts handling of `/users/../todo.txt`, `/users/../../todo.txt` and the URL-encoded `/users/%2e%2e/%2e%2e/todo.txt`, and `res.sendFile.js` covers `fake/../name.txt` and `../name.txt` under a `root`.

All 18 acceptance files import example apps rather than fixtures — `test/acceptance/auth.js` requires `../../examples/auth` and drives the full login/session/restricted flow including cookie extraction.

Seven of the 26 examples have no acceptance test: `online`, `route-middleware`, `search`, `session`, `static-files`, `view-constructor`, `view-locals` — leaving the custom-`View`-constructor extension point exercised only by the example itself.

`test/exports.js` deliberately mutates `express.application`, `express.request` and `express.response` prototypes to prove the extension contract holds — meaning test ordering has real cross-file coupling.
`test/regression.js` is a deliberately tiny guard file — currently one case asserting that throwing after `res.end()` still yields a clean 200 response.

Coverage is produced per matrix cell (`npm run test-ci` → nyc lcovonly), uploaded as `coverage-node-<ver>-<os>` artifacts, then merged in a dedicated `coverage` job with `lcov -a` and pushed to Coveralls.

risk_map.summary: The security-sensitive surface concentrates in four places: proxy trust (which decides whether client-supplied `X-Forwarded-*` headers are believed), JSONP callback sanitisation, file transfer via `res.sendFile`/`res.download`, and dynamic `require()` inside the view system. Blast radius is dominated by `res.send` — `json`, `jsonp`, `sendStatus` and the default `render` callback all funnel through it, so any change there touches nearly every response. Coupling risks come from prototype mutation: `app.handle` re-prototypes live Node objects and mounting re-parents settings chains, so behaviour can change at a distance. Supply-chain posture is strong, but `.npmrc` disables lockfiles, so local installs are not reproducible.

claims.claim: SECURITY — proxy trust: `req.ip`, `req.ips`, `req.protocol`, `req.secure` and `req.host` all believe client-supplied headers whenever `trust proxy fn` returns true; setting `trust proxy` to `true` makes `compileTrust` return a constant-true function, so `X-Forwarded-For`/`-Proto`/`-Host` become fully spoofable.

SECURITY — dynamic require: the `View` constructor derives a module name from the view's file extension and calls `require(mod)`. An application that renders a view name built from user input can drive module resolution, and the thrown errors leak which module was attempted.

SECURITY — JSONP: the callback is taken from `req.query` and filtered with `replace(/[^\[\]\w$.]/g, '')`; correctness of this allowlist plus the `/**/ typeof` wrapper and forced `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff` are the only things standing between `res.jsonp` and reflected script injection.

SECURITY — prototype keys: the `extended` query parser calls `qs.parse` with `allowPrototypes: true`, which is a deliberate compatibility choice that permits keys like `constructor` in parsed query objects.

SECURITY — file IO outside repo root: `res.sendFile` only enforces "absolute path or `root` option" and `encodeURI`; every actual containment check is delegated to the `send` package, so a `send` regression is an Express path-traversal regression.

SECURITY — information disclosure by default: `x-powered-by` is enabled in `defaultConfiguration` and `app.handle` sets the `X-Powered-By: Express` header on every response unless explicitly disabled.

SECURITY — cookie signing depends on a foreign property: `res.cookie` reads `this.req.secret`, which Express never sets; it throws `cookieParser("secret") required for signed cookies` if `cookie-parser` was not installed upstream, making signing silently middleware-order dependent.

BLAST RADIUS — `res.send` is the shared exit for `res.json`, `res.jsonp`, `res.sendStatus` and the default `res.render` callback; the HEAD-vs-body, 204/304/205 header stripping, ETag and Content-Length rules all live in that one function.

FRAGILE COUPLING — mutation of live Node objects: `app.handle` calls `Object.setPrototypeOf` on the actual `IncomingMessage`/`ServerResponse`, and `mounted_app` must manually restore the parent prototypes after a sub-app completes; forgetting that restore silently leaks the child's prototype into sibling middleware.

FRAGILE COUPLING — settings inheritance is by prototype chain (`Object.setPrototypeOf(this.settings, parent.settings)`), guarded by a string symbol `'@@symbol:trust_proxy_default'` that is deleted/redefined in two separate places to preserve back-compat.

PERFORMANCE — synchronous file IO on the request path: `View#resolve` calls `fs.statSync` up to twice per lookup, and `view cache` is only auto-enabled when `NODE_ENV === 'production'`, so non-production deployments stat the filesystem on every render.

PERFORMANCE — `req.query`, `req.host`, `req.protocol` and `req.ip` are non-memoised getters; each access re-parses. Middleware that reads `req.query` repeatedly pays the `qs`/`querystring` cost every time.

extension_points.summary: Express is designed to be extended by mutation rather than by configuration. Three exported prototypes (`express.application`, `express.request`, `express.response`) are public and explicitly documented as mutable by the test suite. Beyond that there are four first-class registries — the template-engine map, the `view` constructor, the compiled-function settings (`etag`/`query parser`/`trust proxy`), and route params — plus mounting, which composes whole apps. The verb table is itself generated from Node's `http.METHODS`, so new HTTP methods appear automatically.

claims.claim: `app.engine(ext, fn)` is the template-engine registry: it normalises the leading dot and stores into `this.engines[extension]`, which `View` consults before falling back to a dynamic `require`.

`app.set('view', CustomViewCtor)` swaps the entire view-resolution class — `app.render` reads `this.get('view')` and does `new View(name, { defaultEngine, root, engines })`, requiring only a `.path` property and a `.render(options, cb)` method.

The three compiler settings all short-circuit on a function argument — `compileETag`, `compileQueryParser` and `compileTrust` each begin with `if (typeof val === 'function') return val`, so any of them can be fully replaced by user code.

`express.application`, `express.request` and `express.response` are exported prototypes and the test suite asserts that mutating them affects all subsequently created apps — the documented monkey-patch seam.
The idiomatic per-app variant of that seam is mutating `app.response` / `app.request` rather than the global prototype, as `examples/mvc` does by defining `app.response.message = function(msg){...}`.

The HTTP verb table is not hardcoded — `exports.methods` maps `require('node:http').METHODS` to lowercase and `methods.forEach` generates both `app[method]` and the per-method registration used by `app.all`.
`app.param(name, fn)` accepts either a single name or an array (recursing per element) and forwards to `this.router.param`, giving a named hook for pre-resolving route parameters.

`app.use(path, subApp)` is the composition primitive: any object with `.handle` and `.set` is treated as a mountable app, receives `mountpath`/`parent`, and emits `'mount'` — which applications may listen to for their own inheritance logic.
`express.Router` and `express.Route` are re-exported from the `router` package, so custom routers can be constructed independently and mounted with `app.use`.

`res.format(obj)` is a per-response dispatch table keyed by MIME type or extension name, with an optional `default` key — the content-negotiation extension point, and itself the mechanism behind `res.redirect`'s body selection.

`app.locals` and `res.locals` are the two data-injection points into rendering; `app.render` merges them in a fixed order with caller options, and `app.locals.settings` is pre-wired so templates can read app settings.

Route organisation patterns are demonstrated as extension idioms rather than framework features: `examples/route-map` builds routes from a nested object literal, and `examples/mvc/lib/boot.js` auto-loads controllers into the app.

agent_handoff.summary: This is a mature, style-conservative library where the diff bar is high and behaviour is pinned by a very large test suite. Read `lib/express.js`, `lib/application.js`, then the method you are changing in `lib/response.js` or `lib/request.js`; the test file name mirrors the API name, so `res.send` changes belong in `test/res.send.js`. The single biggest trap is that `test/acceptance/*` boots the real apps in `examples/`, so editing an example breaks tests in a different directory. Dependencies are installed fresh (no lockfile, no committed `node_modules`), so `npm install` is a required first step.

claims.claim: READ FIRST, in order: `lib/express.js` (the factory and the export surface), `lib/application.js` (settings, `handle`, `use`, `render`), then the specific prototype file you are touching — `lib/response.js` or `lib/request.js`.
SETUP: `node_modules/` is absent and `.npmrc` sets `package-lock=false`, so you must run `npm install` before any test run; there is no build step to run afterwards.

TESTS TO RUN: `npm test` for the full mocha suite (`test/` + `test/acceptance/`), `npm run test-cov` for an HTML coverage report, and `npm run lint` before committing — CI runs lint as a separate required job.

LINT RULES that bite: 2-space `indent` with `MemberExpression: off`, `eqeqeq` with `allow-null`, `eol-last`, `no-trailing-spaces`, and a `no-restricted-globals` rule banning the global `Buffer` — you must write `const { Buffer } = require('node:buffer')`.

STYLE: `lib/` is ES5-flavoured — `var` declarations, `'use strict'` at the top of every file, JSDoc blocks with explicit `@public`/`@private` on every exported member. Match it rather than modernising opportunistically.
NODE BUILTINS are always imported with the `node:` prefix (`node:http`, `node:path`, `node:fs`, `node:net`, `node:querystring`, `node:buffer`, `node:events`) — follow this in new code and in tests.
TEST NAMING is a strict mirror of the API: `test/res.<method>.js`, `test/req.<getter>.js`, `test/app.<method>.js`. A new `res.foo` needs a new `test/res.foo.js`, not an addition to a catch-all file.

TRAP — cross-directory coupling: the 18 files in `test/acceptance/` `require('../../examples/<name>')`, so an edit to an example app fails tests that do not mention it. Check `test/acceptance/` before touching `examples/`.
TRAP — `test/exports.js` permanently mutates `express.application`, `express.request` and `express.response` for the remainder of the mocha process; new global-prototype tests can interact with it.
TRAP — `--check-leaks` is enabled, so any implicit global created during a test (including in `lib/`) fails the run with a leak error rather than an assertion error.
TRAP — the test env sets `NO_DEPRECATION=body-parser,express`, so `depd` warnings you add will be invisible locally; assert on behaviour, not on console output.

SAFE EDIT BOUNDARY — routing, body parsing and static serving are NOT in this repo. Bugs in path matching, `req.params`, `req.body` or directory traversal belong to `router`, `body-parser`, `send` and `serve-static`.

health.summary: Deterministic scan scored 96 source files across simple size, churn, structural, test-adjacency, and performance-risk signals. 12 hotspots surfaced; average score is 8.2/10. Treat these as review leads, not proof of a bug.

qaReadiness.summary: Repo does not expose enough local browser QA structure for a reliable Synthetic QA workflow yet.

readmePreview: FastAPI framework, high performance, easy to learn, fast to code, ready for production --- Documentation: https://fastapi.tiangolo.com Source Code: https://github.com/fastapi/fastapi --- FastAPI is a modern, fast (high-performance), web framework for building

overview.summary: This is the FastAPI framework source repository at version 0.141.1 — a Pydantic v2-only, Starlette-based ASGI web framework whose distinguishing trick is deriving request parsing, validation, serialization and an OpenAPI 3.1 schema from ordinary Python type hints on endpoint functions. This tree is notably ahead of the classic FastAPI architecture: `include_router()` no longer flattens child routes into the parent but stores an `_IncludedRouter` wrapper resolved at match time, the package ships first-class Server-Sent Events (`fastapi/sse.py`) and JSON-Lines streaming, a `app.frontend()` / `router.frontend()` low-priority static-SPA router, and a bundled agent skill at `fastapi/.agents/skills/fastapi/SKILL.md`. The repo is overwhelmingly documentation and tests: 1692 Markdown files across 13 translated locales, 594 test files, and 464 runnable tutorial sources in `docs_src/` that the test suite executes directly. Its audience is Python API developers, and the repo itself enforces 100% line coverage, strict mypy, ty, and Ruff on every push.

system_map.summary: The shipped artifact is the `fastapi/` package (~21k lines across 56 files), a thin-but-deep layer over Starlette and Pydantic v2. `fastapi/applications.py` defines the `FastAPI` app class (subclassing `starlette.applications.Starlette`) and `fastapi/routing.py` — the largest file at 6447 lines — defines `APIRouter`, `APIRoute`, the request handler factory, and the frontend static-file routing. There is no database or storage layer; the only persistent state is in-process route tables and the memoised OpenAPI schema. Everything else in the repo is supporting apparatus: `docs/` (13 locales), `docs_src/` (executable tutorial examples on `PYTHONPATH` during tests), `scripts/` (docs build, translation, release, sponsor tooling), and 23 GitHub Actions workflows. Deployment is a PyPI wheel built by pdm-backend and published via `uv publish` with OIDC trusted publishing; the docs deploy separately to Cloudflare Pages.

claims.claim: The public API surface is re-exported from `fastapi/__init__.py`, which pins `__version__ = "0.141.1"` and exposes exactly 20 names including `FastAPI`, `APIRouter`, `Depends`, `Security`, `BackgroundTasks`, `UploadFile`, `HTTPException`, `WebSocketException` and Starlette's `status` module.

`fastapi/routing.py` (6447 lines) and `fastapi/applications.py` (4774 lines) hold the bulk of the logic; `param_functions.py` is third at 2460 lines but is almost entirely `annotated_doc.Doc` docstrings for `Query`/`Path`/`Header`/`Body`/`Depends`.

Runtime boundaries are ASGI-only: `FastAPI.__call__` injects `root_path` into the scope then delegates to Starlette, and `build_middleware_stack()` composes `ServerErrorMiddleware` → user middleware → `ExceptionMiddleware` → `AsyncExitStackMiddleware` → `self.router`.

FastAPI-specific per-request state is carried in three ASGI scope keys holding `AsyncExitStack`s: `fastapi_middleware_astack` (set by `AsyncExitStackMiddleware` for closing uploaded files), plus `fastapi_inner_astack` and `fastapi_function_astack` set in the vendored `request_response`/`websocket_session` wrappers for request- and function-scoped `yield` dependencies.

Pydantic v1 support has been fully removed: `fastapi/_compat/__init__.py` re-exports only from `.shared` and `.v2`, and `PydanticV1NotSupportedError` is raised from `fastapi/encoders.py` and `fastapi/utils.py` when a v1 model is detected.

Validation is delegated to a single `ModelField` wrapper in `fastapi/_compat/v2.py` that owns a `pydantic.TypeAdapter` and exposes `validate`, `serialize` (dump_python) and `serialize_json` (dump_json).

The CLI entrypoint `fastapi = "fastapi.cli:main"` is a shim that imports `fastapi_cli.cli.main` and raises a RuntimeError telling the user to `pip install "fastapi[standard]"` if the optional package is absent; `fastapi/__main__.py` calls the same function.

Runtime dependencies are minimal and pinned by floor: `starlette>=0.46.0`, `pydantic>=2.9.0`, `typing-extensions>=4.8.0`, `typing-inspection>=0.4.2`, `annotated-doc>=0.0.2`, with Python >= 3.10 required.

`fastapi/staticfiles.py`, `fastapi/templating.py`, `fastapi/testclient.py`, `fastapi/requests.py` and `fastapi/websockets.py` are one-to-three-line re-export shims over Starlette, so those integrations (Jinja2, httpx TestClient) are Starlette's, not FastAPI's.

Build/test/lint commands are shell scripts: `scripts/test.sh` runs `pytest -n auto --dist loadgroup tests scripts/tests/` with `PYTHONPATH=./docs_src`, `scripts/test-cov.sh` adds `--cov --cov-context=test`, and `scripts/lint.sh` runs `mypy fastapi`, `ty check`, `ruff check`, `ruff format --check`.
Release shape: `.github/workflows/publish.yml` triggers on GitHub release publication and runs `uv build` then `uv publish` with `id-token: write` (OIDC trusted publishing, no stored PyPI token).

Docs deploy is a separate pipeline: `deploy-docs.yml` fires on `workflow_run` completion of Build Docs, downloads `docs-site-*` artifacts and pushes to Cloudflare Pages, reporting status through `scripts/deploy_docs_status.py`.

feature_catalog.summary: The user-facing feature set is the decorator API (`@app.get/put/post/delete/options/head/patch/trace`, `@app.websocket`, `@app.middleware`, `@app.exception_handler`), the parameter-declaration vocabulary (`Path`, `Query`, `Header`, `Cookie`, `Body`, `Form`, `File`, `Depends`, `Security`), the auto-generated OpenAPI 3.1 document plus Swagger UI and ReDoc pages, and seven built-in security schemes. This version adds three substantial features beyond classic FastAPI: Server-Sent Events via `response_class=EventSourceResponse`, JSON-Lines streaming from generator endpoints, and `app.frontend()` for serving built SPA assets as low-priority routes. Dependencies gained an explicit `scope` of `"function"` or `"request"`. Two response classes — `ORJSONResponse` and `UJSONResponse` — are now deprecated in favour of a Pydantic `dump_json` fast path.

claims.claim: `FastAPI.setup()` registers up to four non-schema routes at construction: `openapi_url` (default `/openapi.json`), `docs_url` (`/docs`, Swagger UI), `swagger_ui_oauth2_redirect_url`, and `redoc_url` (`/redoc`); each is skipped when its URL is set to `None`.

All eight HTTP verb decorators plus `api_route`, `add_api_route`, `websocket`, `add_api_websocket_route`, `websocket_route`, `on_event`, `middleware`, `exception_handler` and `include_router` are defined on `FastAPI` and mirrored on `APIRouter`.

Server-Sent Events: setting `response_class=EventSourceResponse` on a generator path operation makes the router encode each yielded item into SSE wire format via `format_sse_event`, set `Cache-Control: no-cache` and `X-Accel-Buffering: no`, and inject a `: ping` keepalive comment every `_PING_INTERVAL` (15s) of idleness.

`ServerSentEvent` is a Pydantic model with `data`, `raw_data`, `event`, `id`, `retry`, `comment`; validators reject multi-line `event`/`id` values and null bytes in `id`, and a model validator forbids setting `data` and `raw_data` together.

JSON-Lines streaming: when `is_json_stream` is set, generator endpoints are wrapped into a `StreamingResponse` with media type `application/jsonl`, each item serialized by `_serialize_data` and terminated with `\n`.

`app.frontend(path, directory=..., fallback="auto", check_dir="auto")` serves a built SPA; API routes match first and the frontend is consulted only through `_match_low_priority`, with `fallback="auto"` preferring `404.html` and falling back to `index.html` only for navigation requests that accept `text/html`.

Seven security schemes ship in `fastapi/security/`: `APIKeyQuery`, `APIKeyHeader`, `APIKeyCookie`, `HTTPBasic`, `HTTPBearer`, `HTTPDigest`, `OAuth2` (with `OAuth2PasswordBearer` and `OAuth2AuthorizationCodeBearer`) and `OpenIdConnect`, plus the `OAuth2PasswordRequestForm` dependency and `SecurityScopes`.

Dependency scoping is a first-class feature: `params.Depends` is a frozen dataclass carrying `dependency`, `use_cache` and `scope: Literal["function", "request"] | None`, and `DependencyScopeError` is raised at `get_dependant` time if a request-scoped generator dependency depends on a function-scoped one.
`app.webhooks` is a dedicated `APIRouter` whose routes are documented under the OpenAPI `webhooks` key rather than `paths`.
`strict_content_type` (default `True`) is threaded from app → router → route → handler; when False, a body with no Content-Type header is still parsed as JSON.
`ORJSONResponse` and `UJSONResponse` are marked `@deprecated` with `FastAPIDeprecationWarning`, directing users to declare a return type so Pydantic serializes on the Rust side instead.

`app.dependency_overrides` is a plain dict on the app used as the `dependency_overrides_provider`; `solve_dependencies` re-derives a fresh `Dependant` for any overridden callable so the substitute's own signature is honoured.

data_flow.summary: Input arrives as an ASGI scope. Static declaration time happens first: at decoration, `get_dependant()` walks the endpoint signature with `analyze_param()` and sorts every parameter into `path_params`/`query_params`/`header_params`/`cookie_params`/`body_params`/`dependencies` on a `Dependant` dataclass, each field wrapped in a `ModelField` holding a Pydantic `TypeAdapter`. At request time the handler reads and decodes the body (form vs JSON vs raw bytes), then `solve_dependencies()` recursively resolves sub-dependencies, coerces each parameter group against its `ModelField`, and returns a `SolvedDependency` bundle of values, errors, background tasks and a mutable `Response`. Output flows back through `serialize_response()` (or the streaming serializers) and out as a Starlette `Response`. State owners are the router's route list, the memoised `app.openapi_schema`, and the per-request `AsyncExitStack`s in the ASGI scope.

claims.claim: Body decoding branches on content type: form bodies go through `await request.form()` with `body.close` pushed onto the middleware exit stack; otherwise raw bytes are parsed as JSON only when the Content-Type maintype is `application` and the subtype is `json` or ends in `+json`, else passed through as bytes.

A `json.JSONDecodeError` during body parsing is converted into a `RequestValidationError` with a synthetic `json_invalid` error at loc `("body", e.pos)`; any other parse exception becomes a 400 `HTTPException` with detail 'There was an error parsing the body'.

`solve_dependencies()` resolves sub-dependencies depth-first before extracting path/query/header/cookie values, and memoises each result in `dependency_cache` keyed by `_get_cache_key` — a tuple of `(call, sorted oauth scopes, computed scope)` — so the same dependency called twice in one request runs once unless `use_cache=False`.

Generator dependencies are entered as context managers by `_solve_generator`: async generators via `asynccontextmanager`, sync generators via `contextmanager_in_threadpool`, and pushed onto `fastapi_inner_astack` unless the dependency declares `scope="function"`, in which case `fastapi_function_astack` is used so it tears down before the response is sent.

`contextmanager_in_threadpool` deliberately gives `__exit__` its own `CapacityLimiter(1)` so a blocking teardown cannot deadlock against the shared AnyIO threadpool used by a connection pool inside the dependency.

Form bodies flow through `_extract_form_body`, which reads `UploadFile` values into `bytes` when the declared annotation is bytes, expands sequence-of-bytes fields, and passes through any unmatched form keys as single values or lists.

`request_body_to_args` collapses to a single un-embedded field when `len(body_fields) == 1 and not embed_body_fields`, and in that case a `BaseModel`-annotated form body is exploded into its model fields before validation.

Response serialization has a fast path: when a `response_field` exists and no custom `response_class` was supplied, `serialize_response(dump_json=True)` calls `ModelField.serialize_json` and the bytes are wrapped in a bare `Response(media_type="application/json")`, skipping the dict → `json.dumps` round trip.

Headers set on the injected `Response` object by dependencies are merged into the final response via `response.headers.raw.extend(solved_result.response.headers.raw)` on every branch (SSE, JSONL, raw stream, and normal).
When `is_body_allowed_for_status_code(status_code)` is false (1xx, 204, 205, 304), the serialized body is discarded by setting `response.body = b""`.

Validation failures never reach the endpoint: `errors` accumulated by `solve_dependencies` short-circuit the handler and raise `RequestValidationError`, which the default handler renders as HTTP 422 with `{"detail": jsonable_encoder(exc.errors())}`.

The OpenAPI document is produced once and cached on `app.openapi_schema`, invalidated by comparing `self.router._get_routes_version()` — a recursive counter that sums `_routes_version` across all `_IncludedRouter` children — against `_openapi_routes_version`.

behavior_traces.summary: Three flows dominate: application construction, a normal HTTP request, and OpenAPI generation. Construction is eager — dependants and response fields are computed at decoration time, so route registration errors surface at import. A request walks ASGI middleware, router matching (now indirected through `_IncludedRouter` for included routers), the exit-stack-wrapping `request_response` shim, dependency solving, endpoint invocation, and serialization. Streaming requests diverge at the handler into three branches (SSE, JSONL, raw generator). WebSockets follow a parallel but simpler path with no body parsing and no response serialization.

claims.claim: Startup trace: `FastAPI.__init__` assigns metadata, asserts `title` and `version` when `openapi_url` is truthy, constructs `self.router = APIRouter(...)` with `dependency_overrides_provider=self`, seeds three default `exception_handlers`, and finally calls `self.setup()` which registers the `/openapi.json`, `/docs`, oauth2-redirect and `/redoc` routes.

Route registration trace: `@app.get(...)` → `app.router.add_api_route` → `APIRoute.__init__` → `_populate_api_route_state(...)` (which builds `dependant`, `body_field`, `response_field`, `stream_item_field`, `unique_id`) → `self.app = request_response(self.get_route_handler())`.

Lifespan trace: `APIRouter.app` routes `scope["type"] == "lifespan"` to `self.lifespan`; when no custom lifespan is given, `_DefaultLifespan` (re-vendored after Starlette removed it) calls `router._startup()` / `router._shutdown()` so `on_startup`/`on_shutdown` handlers still work, and `include_router` merges child lifespans via `_merge_lifespan_context`.

Matching trace for an included router: `APIRouter.app` iterates `self.routes`, an `_IncludedRouter` entry answers `matches()` by building `_EffectiveRouteContext` objects that apply the accumulated prefix/tags/dependencies, then `handle()` dispatches through `_handle_selected`.

Request trace (happy path): `request_response.app` creates the `Request`, opens `fastapi_inner_astack` and `fastapi_function_astack`, awaits the handler, sends the response, then asserts `response_awaited` — raising a `FastAPIError` naming the bare-`except`-in-a-yield-dependency footgun if the stack unwound without sending.

Handler trace: `get_request_handler.app` → `_extract_endpoint_context(dependant.call)` → body read → `solve_dependencies(...)` → branch on `is_sse_stream` / `is_json_stream` / generator / plain → `run_endpoint_function` → `serialize_response` → `_build_response_args` → Response.

Sync endpoints are offloaded: `run_endpoint_function` calls `run_in_threadpool(dependant.call, **values)` when `_is_coroutine_callable(dependant.call)` is false, and `serialize_response` likewise runs `field.validate` in a threadpool for sync endpoints.

SSE trace: the generator is obtained, wrapped in `_sse_producer_cm()` entered on `fastapi_inner_astack` (so teardown is structured rather than via `GeneratorExit`), each item routed through `_serialize_sse_item` → `format_sse_event`, then yielded through `_sse_with_checkpoints` which `await anyio.sleep(0)` after each chunk so cancellation can be delivered.

WebSocket trace: `websocket_session` opens the same two exit stacks, `get_websocket_app.app` builds an endpoint context labelled `WS <path>`, calls `solve_dependencies` with no body, raises `WebSocketRequestValidationError` on errors, and otherwise awaits the endpoint directly — there is no response serialization step.
WebSocket validation failures close the socket with code 1008 (`WS_1008_POLICY_VIOLATION`) and the encoded errors as the reason, via `websocket_request_validation_exception_handler`.

Frontend fallback trace: `_FrontendStaticFiles.get_response` rejects non-GET/HEAD with 405 or 404, looks up the static resource, redirects directory hits missing a trailing slash, then applies the `404.html` / `index.html` fallback — the latter only if `_is_frontend_navigation_request` finds `text/html` or `application/xhtml+xml` with non-zero q in the Accept header.

OpenAPI trace: `app.openapi()` → `get_openapi(...)` → `get_fields_from_routes` (collects body/response/stream/param `ModelField`s across `iter_route_contexts`) → `get_flat_models_from_fields` → `get_model_name_map` → `get_definitions` → per-route `get_openapi_path` → `jsonable_encoder(OpenAPI(**output), by_alias=True, exclude_none=True)`.

testing_signals.summary: Testing is the repo's centre of gravity: 594 files under `tests/`, 213 top-level `test_*.py` modules, plus `tests/test_tutorial/` mirroring the 77 directories of `docs_src/` so every documented example is executed. The stack is pytest 9 with `pytest-xdist` (`-n auto --dist loadgroup`), `anyio[trio]`, `inline-snapshot` (used in ~299 files), `dirty-equals` (~31 files), `pytest-timeout` at 20s, and `filterwarnings = ["error"]`. CI enforces `coverage report --fail-under=100` over `fastapi`, `tests` and `docs_src` combined, across a matrix of Windows/macOS/Ubuntu and Python 3.10–3.14t, including free-threaded builds and a Starlette-from-git leg. Performance has its own gates via CodSpeed wall-clock and memory benchmarks. The notable gap is that everything runs through the in-process `TestClient`; there is no test that boots a real uvicorn server.

claims.claim: The test command is `pytest -n auto --dist loadgroup tests scripts/tests/` with `PYTHONPATH=./docs_src`, so tutorial modules are importable by name from the tutorial tests.

pytest is configured with `--strict-config --strict-markers --ignore=docs_src`, `strict_xfail = true`, `filterwarnings = ["error"]` and a 20-second per-test timeout, so any unexpected warning fails the suite.

Coverage is measured over three source roots (`docs_src`, `tests`, `fastapi`) with `parallel = true` and per-runner `CONTEXT`, and the `coverage-combine` CI job ends with `coverage report --fail-under=100`.

The CI matrix covers Windows and macOS on Python 3.14 and 3.14t (free-threaded) plus targeted Ubuntu/macOS legs for 3.10 (with `uv-resolution: lowest-direct` and a forced `pydantic==2.9.0`), 3.12, 3.13 and 3.14, and a `starlette-git` leg installing Starlette from main.

A dedicated `regression-test` job checks out the PR base revision, applies only the PR's test diff, and warns via `::warning::` if the changed tests already pass without the code change — an automated 'does this test actually prove the fix' gate.
Performance regressions are gated by two CodSpeed jobs: `pytest tests/benchmarks --codspeed` in simulation mode and `pytest tests/memory_benchmarks --codspeed` in memory mode.

`inline-snapshot` is the dominant assertion style for OpenAPI and error payloads, appearing in roughly 299 test files, with CI setting `INLINE_SNAPSHOT_DEFAULT_FLAGS: review` to prevent silent snapshot rewrites.

The new frontend feature is densely covered: `tests/test_frontend.py` has 40+ tests including Accept-header q-value parsing, path-segment boundary matching, trailing-slash normalization, dependency ordering across nested `include_router`, and `PermissionError`/`ENAMETOOLONG` lookup failures.

Streaming has dedicated suites for SSE (`tests/test_sse.py`), cancellation (`tests/test_stream_cancellation.py`), item validation errors (`tests/test_stream_json_validation_error.py`), bare types and status codes, plus tutorial tests under `tests/test_tutorial/test_server_sent_events` and `test_stream_json_lines`.

Security coverage is per-scheme and per-variant — around 30 files spanning `test_security_http_basic*`, `test_security_api_key_*`, `test_security_oauth2*`, `test_security_scopes*`, `test_security_openid_connect*`, plus `test_webhooks_security.py` and `test_top_level_security_scheme_in_openapi.py`.

Performance claims in the code are pinned by behavioural tests: `tests/test_dump_json_fast_path.py` patches `starlette.responses.json.dumps` and asserts it is never called on the default-response-class path.

Static analysis is part of the gate, not optional: `.pre-commit-config.yaml` runs ruff check/format, `mypy fastapi` (with `strict = true`), `ty check` (`error-on-warning = true`), typos, and `zizmor` over `.github/workflows/`.

risk_map.summary: As a library, the dangerous surfaces are file IO (the new frontend static server), auth scheme edge cases, and the streaming/exit-stack machinery where resource teardown is subtle. The frontend server is the newest and widest-blast-radius addition: it reads arbitrary files from a user-supplied directory on every unmatched request. The included-router rework is the deepest structural change and introduces a per-request handler rebuild plus a ContextVar hand-off that the code itself flags as temporary. Two caches — `_endpoint_context_cache` and the `lru_cache`d callable classifiers — are keyed by object identity, which is correct only as long as the keyed objects outlive the cache. Repo-level supply-chain risk is actively managed: all Actions are SHA-pinned, `permissions: {}` is the default, `persist-credentials: false` on every checkout, and zizmor lints the workflows.

claims.claim: `_FrontendStaticFiles` serves files from a user-supplied directory on every request that no API route matched; it mitigates traversal by normalizing the path (`os.path.normpath(os.path.join(*path.split("/")))`), delegating to Starlette's `lookup_path`, and passing `follow_symlink=False`, but the blast radius of a bug here is arbitrary file disclosure.

`_lookup_path` maps a `PermissionError` on the filesystem to an HTTP 401 response, which conflates a server-side filesystem permission problem with a client authentication failure and can leak the existence of unreadable paths.

`APIRoute.handle` rebuilds the entire request handler — `request_response(self.get_route_handler())`, which re-runs `get_request_handler` — on every single request whenever an `_EffectiveRouteContext` is present, i.e. for all routes reached through `include_router`.

The effective-route context is passed from `handle()` to `get_route_handler()` through a module-level ContextVar rather than an argument, and the code carries a `TODO: Replace or deprecate this no-scope hook` — any subclass overriding `get_route_handler()` interacts with this implicitly.

`_endpoint_context_cache` is an unbounded module-level `dict[int, EndpointContext]` keyed by `id(func)`; entries are never evicted, so a process that creates endpoint callables dynamically grows the dict without bound and could in principle collide on a recycled `id`.

The callable classifiers `_is_gen_callable`/`_is_async_gen_callable`/`_is_coroutine_callable` use `lru_cache(maxsize=4096)` keyed by a `_CallIdentity` whose `__hash__` is `id(self.call)`, so the cache holds a strong reference to every classified callable and identity reuse after GC is the correctness assumption.

`HTTPBasic.__call__` base64-decodes the Authorization header and splits on `:`; it returns the raw username and password with no timing-safe comparison anywhere in the framework — constant-time credential checking is left entirely to the application.

Every security scheme has an `auto_error=False` mode that returns `None` instead of raising 401; a dependency written against that mode that forgets to check for `None` silently authenticates everyone.

The default Swagger UI and ReDoc pages load JavaScript and CSS from `cdn.jsdelivr.net` (and Google Fonts for ReDoc) with no SRI hashes, so `/docs` and `/redoc` execute third-party CDN code by default in every FastAPI app.

Swagger UI parameter injection is defended by `_html_safe_json`, which escapes `<`, `>` and `&` before interpolating user-supplied `swagger_ui_parameters` and `init_oauth` into a `<script>` block — but `oauth2_redirect_url` is interpolated into the same script with no escaping.

`_extract_endpoint_context` calls `inspect.getsourcefile` and `getsourcelines`, embedding absolute server file paths into `ValidationException.__str__`; these appear in logs and in `ResponseValidationError` tracebacks but not in the 422 JSON body, which only serializes `exc.errors()`.

`request_response` detects a swallowed exception in a `yield` dependency only after the fact, by checking a `response_awaited` flag and raising a `FastAPIError` with a docs link — a heuristic guard rather than a structural fix.

extension_points.summary: FastAPI's extension model is almost entirely composition and subclassing rather than registries. The three canonical hooks are `route_class` on `APIRouter` (swap `APIRoute` for a subclass overriding `get_route_handler`), `dependency_overrides` (a dict keyed by the original callable), and `exception_handlers` (a dict keyed by exception type or status code). Beyond those, `SecurityBase` is the contract for new auth schemes, `generate_unique_id_function` controls operation IDs for client generators, `default_response_class` and `response_class` control output encoding, and `openapi_extra` plus overriding `app.openapi()` let you post-process the schema. The `DefaultPlaceholder`/`Default()` sentinel is the mechanism that lets app → router → route parameter inheritance distinguish 'not set' from 'explicitly set to the default value'.

claims.claim: `APIRouter(route_class=...)` accepts any `APIRoute` subclass; the documented pattern is to override `get_route_handler()` to wrap the returned coroutine, and `tests/test_custom_route_class.py` plus `docs_src/custom_request_and_route/` exercise it.

New authentication schemes plug in by subclassing `SecurityBase` — a two-attribute protocol (`model: SecurityBaseModel`, `scheme_name: str`) — which `_is_security_scheme` detects via `isinstance` on the unwrapped callable to feed OpenAPI `securitySchemes`.

`dependency_overrides` is the testing seam: any object with a `.dependency_overrides` dict can be passed as `dependency_overrides_provider`, and `solve_dependencies` rebuilds the `Dependant` from the substitute callable so its own parameters are resolved.

`exception_handlers` is a mutable dict keyed by exception class or the ints 500 / `Exception`; `build_middleware_stack` splits the 500/`Exception` entry out as `ServerErrorMiddleware`'s handler and hands the rest to `ExceptionMiddleware`.

`generate_unique_id_function` (default `generate_unique_id`, which slugifies `route.name + path_format + method`) is inheritable app → router → route and is the hook for client-generator-friendly operation IDs.

The `DefaultPlaceholder` / `Default()` pattern plus `get_value_or_default` is how a router's setting overrides an app's only when explicitly provided — `Default(JSONResponse)` is not the same as passing `JSONResponse`.

`_RouterIncludeContext.for_include` and `.combine` are the single place where inherited router attributes (prefix, tags, dependencies, responses, callbacks, deprecated, include_in_schema, unique-id fn, strict_content_type) are merged — new inheritable router options must be added to both methods.

`_low_priority_routes` on `APIRouter` is a general extension slot, not frontend-specific: `frontend()` appends a `_FrontendRouteGroup` to it, and `_match_low_priority` consults the list only after normal matching and redirect-slashes handling fail.

Custom response encodings plug in by subclassing `starlette.responses.Response` and passing it as `response_class`; `EventSourceResponse` is itself just such a marker subclass, detected with `lenient_issubclass(actual_response_class, EventSourceResponse)`.

OpenAPI can be extended at three levels: per-operation `openapi_extra` on a route, whole-document post-processing by reassigning `app.openapi`, and swapping the `openapi_url`/`docs_url`/`redoc_url` routes by passing `None` and registering your own.

`jsonable_encoder` accepts `custom_encoder` and `sqlalchemy_safe`, and the class→encoder mapping is precomputed by `generate_encoders_by_class_tuples(ENCODERS_BY_TYPE)`, which is the hook for adding new type serializers.

Middleware plugs in three ways: the `middleware=[Middleware(...)]` constructor argument, `app.add_middleware(...)`, and the `@app.middleware("http")` decorator which wraps the function in `BaseHTTPMiddleware`.

agent_handoff.summary: Read `fastapi/.agents/skills/fastapi/SKILL.md` first — it is the project's own statement of intended API style and is authoritative for any user-facing example you write. Then read `fastapi/routing.py` (specifically `get_request_handler`, `include_router`, and the `_IncludedRouter`/`_EffectiveRouteContext` pair) and `fastapi/dependencies/utils.py` (`get_dependant`, `analyze_param`, `solve_dependencies`), because nearly every behavioural change lands in one of those. The hard constraints are 100% coverage, strict mypy plus ty, `filterwarnings = ["error"]`, and `inline-snapshot` review mode — a change that is functionally right but leaves a line uncovered or emits a warning will fail CI. Dependency files are off-limits to non-org contributors and enforced by a workflow that auto-closes such PRs.

claims.claim: Read first, in order: `fastapi/.agents/skills/fastapi/SKILL.md` (conventions), `fastapi/applications.py#L873-1164` (app construction), `fastapi/routing.py#L375-762` (the request handler), `fastapi/dependencies/utils.py#L271-733` (dependency graph + solving), `fastapi/_compat/v2.py#L114-235` (ModelField).
Run `bash scripts/test.sh` for the suite and `bash scripts/lint.sh` before proposing a change; `scripts/format.sh` applies `ruff --fix` and `ruff format` across `fastapi tests docs_src scripts`.

Any new library code must be covered — CI runs `coverage report --fail-under=100` over `fastapi`, `tests` and `docs_src` combined, so genuinely unreachable branches need an explicit `# pragma: no cover` (the existing convention in `fastapi/dependencies/models.py`).

New documentation examples belong in `docs_src/<topic>/tutorialNNN_py310.py` with a matching `tests/test_tutorial/test_<topic>/test_tutorialNNN.py`; `docs_src` is on `PYTHONPATH` during tests and excluded from pytest collection.

Snapshot assertions must not be silently regenerated: CI sets `INLINE_SNAPSHOT_DEFAULT_FLAGS: review`, and the `[tool.inline-snapshot]` fix/create flags in `pyproject.toml` are commented out on purpose.

Do not edit `pyproject.toml` or `uv.lock` on behalf of an outside contributor: `guard-dependencies.yml` auto-comments and closes any PR touching them unless the author is an org MEMBER/OWNER or `dependabot[bot]`.

Only `docs/en/` is hand-edited; the `ensure-non-translated` pre-commit hook rejects modifications to non-English docs outside the translated set, and `README.md` is generated from `docs/en/docs/index.md` by the `generate-readme` hook.

Trap: `include_router` no longer copies routes. Code that assumes `app.routes` is a flat list of `APIRoute` objects will silently miss included routes — iterate with `routing.iter_route_contexts(routes)` and unwrap via `RouteContext`, the way `get_fields_from_routes` does.

Trap: after adding or mutating routes at runtime you must go through `add_route`/`add_api_route`/`include_router`/`frontend`, all of which call `_mark_routes_changed()`; appending directly to `router.routes` will leave the cached `app.openapi_schema` stale.

Trap: three distinct `AsyncExitStack`s live in the scope with different lifetimes — `fastapi_middleware_astack` (files), `fastapi_inner_astack` (request-scoped yield deps and the SSE producer), `fastapi_function_astack` (function-scoped yield deps). Picking the wrong one changes when teardown runs relative to the response being sent.
Trap: every new streaming code path needs an `await anyio.sleep(0)` checkpoint after each yielded chunk, or client-disconnect cancellation is never delivered — the existing sites cite issue #14680.

Safe edit boundary: `fastapi/staticfiles.py`, `fastapi/templating.py`, `fastapi/testclient.py`, `fastapi/requests.py`, `fastapi/websockets.py`, `fastapi/logger.py` and `fastapi/middleware/*.py` (except `asyncexitstack.py`) are pure re-exports — behaviour changes belong upstream in Starlette, not here.

name: flask

health.summary: Deterministic scan scored 35 source files across simple size, churn, structural, test-adjacency, and performance-risk signals. 8 hotspots surfaced; average score is 7.5/10. Treat these as review leads, not proof of a bug.

qaReadiness.summary: Repo does not expose enough local browser QA structure for a reliable Synthetic QA workflow yet.

readmePreview: Flask Flask is a lightweight [WSGI] web application framework.

overview.summary: Flask is the Pallets WSGI web framework — a thin, opinion-light composition layer over Werkzeug (routing, request/response, dev server), Jinja (templating), itsdangerous (signed session cookies), Click (CLI) and Blinker (signals), distributed as the `flask` package plus a `flask` console script. This checkout is the unreleased 3.2.0.dev line on `main`, whose headline change is the merger of `RequestContext` into a single `AppContext`: one context object now carries app, `g`, request, session and URL adapter, is pushed once per request and per CLI command, and is threaded explicitly as a `ctx` first argument through `dispatch_request`, `full_dispatch_request`, `finalize_request`, `preprocess_request`, `process_response` and the teardown methods. The codebase is deliberately split into a sans-IO core (`src/flask/sansio/`) that alternative implementations such as Quart reuse, and IO-bound subclasses (`app.py`, `blueprints.py`) that add WSGI, Click groups and file serving. It targets Python 3.10+, is fully typed (`py.typed`, strict mypy + pyright), and ships its own tutorial, JavaScript and Celery example applications.

system_map.summary: The library entrypoints are the `flask` package namespace (`src/flask/__init__.py` re-exports the public API), the `flask` console script wired to `flask.cli:main`, and `python -m flask` via `__main__.py`. Runtime is split across a sans-IO layer (`Scaffold` → `App` → `Blueprint` in `src/flask/sansio/`) that holds registries and setup logic with no IO, and the IO layer (`Flask`, `Blueprint`, `cli`, `helpers`, `templating`) that performs WSGI dispatch, file serving and server startup. There is no database or persistence layer; the only durable state Flask owns is the signed session cookie written by `SecureCookieSessionInterface`. External integrations are all Pallets-family libraries pinned in `pyproject.toml` dependencies, plus optional `asgiref` (async views) and `python-dotenv` (env files). Build is flit_core; test/lint/type/docs orchestration is tox driven by uv, executed in GitHub Actions.

claims.claim: `src/flask/__init__.py` is the public API surface: 39 explicit `X as X` re-exports covering `Flask`, `Blueprint`, `Config`, the five context proxies, all 10 signals, and the `render_template`/`stream_template` family — nothing is exported implicitly.

The console script is declared as `flask = "flask.cli:main"` under `[project.scripts]`, and `src/flask/__main__.py` is a three-line shim (`from .cli import main; main()`) so `python -m flask` and `flask` share one code path.

The sans-IO boundary is documented in-tree: `src/flask/sansio/README.md` states the folder must do no IO, must not be on a likely IO path, and must not use the Flask globals — which is why `sansio/app.py` declares `default_config` and `response_class` as bare annotations and lets `Flask` in `app.py` supply them.

Class hierarchy is `Scaffold` (shared route/handler registration, static folder, `find_package`) → `App` (config, url_map, blueprints dict, extensions dict, template filters/tests/globals) → `Flask` (WSGI, Click group, sessions, file serving); `Blueprint` follows the same sansio → IO split.

All context state lives in one `AppContext` object holding `app`, `g`, `url_adapter`, `_request`, `_session`, `_flashes` and `_after_request_functions`, stored in the single `ContextVar` `_cv_app` declared in `globals.py`; there is no second request-level ContextVar.

The five public proxies (`app_ctx`, `current_app`, `g`, `request`, `session`) are all `werkzeug.local.LocalProxy` instances over the same `_cv_app`, differing only by attribute name and unbound-error message (`_no_app_msg` vs `_no_req_msg`).

The only persistence layer is the signed cookie: `SecureCookieSessionInterface` builds a `URLSafeTimedSerializer` with salt `"cookie-session"`, hmac key derivation, lazily-resolved SHA-1 digest, and the `TaggedJSONSerializer` payload serializer.

Runtime dependencies are exactly six Pallets-ecosystem packages (blinker≥1.9.0, click≥8.1.3, itsdangerous≥2.2.0, jinja2≥3.1.2, markupsafe≥2.1.1, werkzeug≥3.1.0) with `async` (asgiref) and `dotenv` (python-dotenv) as optional extras.

Build backend is `flit_core>=3.11,<4` with `[tool.flit.module] name = "flask"`, and the sdist explicitly bundles `docs/`, `examples/`, `tests/`, `CHANGES.rst` and `uv.lock` while excluding `docs/_build/`.

Developer commands are tox environments: `tox run` (pytest per Python version), `-e style` (pre-commit all files), `-e typing` (mypy then pyright), `-e docs` (`sphinx-build -E -W -b dirhtml docs docs/_build/dirhtml`), plus `tests-min` and `tests-dev` which pip-install pinned-minimum and git-main dependency sets respectively.

CI is four GitHub Actions workflows: `tests.yaml` (12-way matrix incl. 3.15, free-threaded 3.14t, Windows, Mac, PyPy, min and dev deps, plus a separate mypy/pyright `typing` job), `pre-commit.yaml`, `publish.yaml` (tag-triggered `uv build` → draft GH release → PyPI trusted publishing), and `zizmor.yaml` for Actions security analysis.

Docs are Sphinx `dirhtml` built by Read the Docs using an asdf-installed uv and the `docs` dependency group; 34 top-level doc pages exist including `lifecycle.rst`, `appcontext.rst`, `reqcontext.rst` and `web-security.rst`.

feature_catalog.summary: As a framework, Flask's user-facing features are its decorator registries, its CLI subcommands, and its request/response conveniences. Route registration spans `@route` plus seven method shortcuts including the newly added `@app.query` for HTTP QUERY; class-based views come via `View`/`MethodView`. The `flask` CLI ships `run`, `shell` and `routes` built in, discovers app-provided commands through `app.cli`/`blueprint.cli`, and loads third-party commands from the `flask.commands` entry point group. Response handling covers strings, bytes, dicts, lists, generators, tuples, WSGI callables and Response objects; JSON is routed through a swappable `JSONProvider`. Sessions, flashing, file sending, streaming, signals and blueprint nesting round out the surface.

claims.claim: Seven HTTP-method route shortcuts are generated through `Scaffold._method_route`: `get`, `query`, `post`, `put`, `delete`, `patch` (plus `route`); `query` is new in 3.2 for the HTTP QUERY method and is also listed in `views.http_method_funcs`.

`flask run` exposes `--host/-h` (default 127.0.0.1), `--port/-p` (5000), `--cert`/`--key`, `--reload/--no-reload`, `--debugger/--no-debugger`, `--with-threads/--without-threads`, `--extra-files` and `--exclude-patterns`, and inserts `--debug` as its first parameter after definition.

`flask shell` builds an interactive REPL banner from `current_app.import_name` and `instance_path`, honours `PYTHONSTARTUP`, wires `rlcompleter.Completer` against the shell context rather than `__main__`, then calls `code.interact`.
`flask routes` supports `--sort` over `endpoint|methods|domain|rule|match` and `--all-methods`, hides HEAD/OPTIONS by default, and renders a padded ASCII table computed from per-column max widths.

The root CLI group is `FlaskGroup`, which registers three eager options in order (`--env-file`, `--app`, `--debug`) so dotenv loading happens before app import, and sets `auto_envvar_prefix="FLASK"` so every option is also settable via `FLASK_*` env vars.

App discovery supports four forms: explicit `module:name`, `module:factory(args)` with `ast.literal_eval`-parsed arguments, auto-detection of `app`/`application`/`create_app`/`make_app`, and implicit `wsgi.py` then `app.py` in the CWD.

`Flask.make_response` accepts str/bytes/bytearray, any iterator (streaming), dict and list (auto-JSON via `self.json.response`), `BaseResponse` subclasses, arbitrary WSGI callables, and 2- or 3-tuples of `(body, status)`, `(body, headers)` or `(body, status, headers)`.

Class-based views: `View.as_view` supports `init_every_request=False` for a shared instance, applies `cls.decorators` in order, and copies `methods`/`provide_automatic_options` onto the generated function; `MethodView.__init_subclass__` auto-derives `methods` from defined handler names and falls back from HEAD to GET.

Message flashing writes `session["_flashes"]` via a read-append-reassign pattern (deliberately not `setdefault`, so external session backends stay in sync) and emits the `message_flashed` signal; `get_flashed_messages` caches into `app_ctx._flashes` so repeat calls in one request are stable.

Ten Blinker signals are defined in one namespace: template-rendered, before-render-template, request-started, request-finished, request-tearing-down, got-request-exception, appcontext-tearing-down, appcontext-pushed, appcontext-popped and message-flashed.

Async views are opt-in: `ensure_sync` returns plain functions unchanged and wraps coroutine functions via `async_to_sync`, which imports `asgiref.sync.async_to_sync` and raises "Install Flask with the 'async' extra" if asgiref is missing.

Config can be populated six ways: `from_envvar`, `from_prefixed_env` (JSON-decoded `FLASK_*` vars with `__` nesting), `from_pyfile` (exec'd as a module), `from_object` (uppercase attrs only), `from_file` (pluggable loader, text or binary) and `from_mapping`; `get_namespace` extracts prefixed subsets.

data_flow.summary: Input boundaries are the WSGI environ, the process environment (`FLASK_*`, dotenv files), config files, and the request cookie jar. A WSGI environ becomes a `Request` in `AppContext.from_environ`, which also stamps `request.json_module = app.json` so body JSON decoding uses the app's provider. The `AppContext` is the single state owner for the duration of a request: it holds `g`, the lazily opened session, the bound `MapAdapter`, collected `after_this_request` callbacks and cached flashes. Output boundaries are the `Response` returned to the WSGI server, the `Set-Cookie` session header written in `process_response`, rendered template strings, and log records emitted to `wsgi.errors` or stderr. Config flows one way: `default_config` → `Config` dict → `ConfigAttribute` descriptors (`app.testing`, `app.secret_key`, `app.permanent_session_lifetime`) and per-request property lookups on `Request`/`Response`.

claims.claim: The environ→Request transform happens in `AppContext.from_environ`, which constructs `app.request_class(environ)` and immediately assigns `request.json_module = app.json`, so `request.get_json()` uses the app's JSON provider rather than stdlib json.

The URL adapter is built in `AppContext.__init__` (not at push time) via `app.create_url_adapter`, and any `HTTPException` raised there is stashed on `request.routing_exception` instead of propagating.

`create_url_adapter` applies `TRUSTED_HOSTS` to `request.trusted_hosts` and then recomputes `request.host` through `werkzeug.wsgi.get_host` before binding — host validation happens on this path, before routing.

Session data flows cookie → `SecureCookieSessionInterface.open_session` → `URLSafeTimedSerializer.loads(val, max_age=PERMANENT_SESSION_LIFETIME)` → `SecureCookieSession`; a `BadSignature` silently yields a fresh empty session rather than an error.

Session writes are deferred to `process_response`, which calls `save_session` only when `is_null_session` is false, and `save_session` adds `Vary: Cookie` whenever `session.accessed` is set, deletes the cookie when an emptied session is modified, and otherwise gates on `should_set_cookie`.

Session values are serialized by `TaggedJSONSerializer`, which round-trips non-JSON Python types through single-key tag dicts — ` di` (dict), ` t` (tuple), ` b` (base64 bytes), ` m` (Markup), ` u` (UUID), ` d` (http-date datetime).

Config resolution order is `default_config` copy → `DEBUG` overwritten from `get_debug_flag()` (the `FLASK_DEBUG` env var) → `Config(root_path, defaults)`, with `root_path` swapped to `instance_path` when `instance_relative_config=True`.

Env-file input precedence is: variables already in `os.environ` win, then `-e/--env-file`, then `.env`, then `.flaskenv` — implemented by merging dicts in that order in `load_dotenv` and skipping keys already present in `os.environ`.

Per-request body limits read through `current_app.config` at access time rather than being copied onto the request: `max_content_length`, `max_form_memory_size` and `max_form_parts` each check a private override, then fall back to `MAX_CONTENT_LENGTH` / `MAX_FORM_MEMORY_SIZE` (500_000) / `MAX_FORM_PARTS` (1_000).

Template context is assembled in `update_template_context`: app-level then reversed blueprint-level context processors run, and the caller's explicit `render_template(**context)` values are re-applied last from a saved copy so they always win.

The default template context processor replaces the `request` and `g` proxies with concrete objects for speed but deliberately leaves `session` as a proxy, because touching it would set `session.accessed` and force a `Vary: Cookie` header.

`send_file`/`send_from_directory` funnel through `_prepare_send_file_kwargs`, which injects `environ`, `USE_X_SENDFILE`, `response_class`, `_root_path` and defaults `max_age` to `app.get_send_file_max_age` before delegating to Werkzeug.

behavior_traces.summary: Three flows dominate: application construction, WSGI request dispatch, and CLI invocation. Construction is `Flask.__init__` → `App.__init__` → `Scaffold.__init__`, ending with an auto-registered static route that holds only a weakref to the app. Request dispatch is `__call__` → `wsgi_app` → `AppContext.push` (session open, then routing) → `full_dispatch_request` → `preprocess_request` → `dispatch_request` → `finalize_request` → `process_response` (session save) → `ctx.pop` (teardowns). CLI invocation is `main` → `FlaskGroup.make_context` (sets `FLASK_RUN_FROM_CLI`) → eager `--env-file`/`--app` callbacks → `ScriptInfo.load_app` → command body with an app context pushed via `ctx.with_resource`.

claims.claim: Startup: `Flask.__init__` calls `super().__init__` (App → Scaffold), creates `self.cli = cli.AppGroup()` named after the app, then — if `has_static_folder` — asserts `bool(static_host) == host_matching` and registers `f"{static_url_path}/<path:filename>"` with a `weakref.ref(self)` closure to avoid an app↔view reference cycle (issue #3761).

Startup: `App.__init__` resolves `instance_path` (rejecting relative paths), builds `config` via `make_config`, instantiates `aborter`, `json_provider_class(self)`, the empty `blueprints`/`extensions` dicts, `url_map_class(host_matching=...)`, and sets `_got_first_request = False`.

Request: `Flask.__call__` → `wsgi_app(environ, start_response)` creates the context with `self.request_context(environ)`, pushes it, dispatches, and in `finally` restores it for the debugger via `environ["werkzeug.debug.preserve_context"]` before `ctx.pop(error)`.

Request: `AppContext.push` increments `_push_count`, returns early if already pushed, sets `_cv_app`, sends `appcontext_pushed`, then opens the session via `_get_session()` *before* calling `match_request()` — ordering that lets custom URL converters read the session.

Request: `full_dispatch_request` sets `_got_first_request = True` (freezing setup methods), sends `request_started`, runs `preprocess_request`, short-circuits to `finalize_request` if a `before_request` returned non-None, otherwise calls `dispatch_request`, catching exceptions into `handle_user_exception`.

Request: `preprocess_request` runs `url_value_preprocessors` for `(None, *reversed(req.blueprints))` first, then `before_request_funcs` in the same order — app-level before blueprint-level, outermost blueprint first.

Request: `dispatch_request` raises any stored `routing_exception` through `raise_routing_exception`, returns `make_default_options_response` for automatic OPTIONS, and otherwise calls `ensure_sync(self.view_functions[rule.endpoint])(**view_args)`.

Request: `process_response` runs `ctx._after_request_functions` (from `after_this_request`) first, then app+blueprint `after_request_funcs` in reverse registration order over `chain(request.blueprints, (None,))`, then saves the session.

Teardown: `AppContext.pop` decrements `_push_count`, returns while still nested, then under `_CollectErrors` runs `do_teardown_request`, `request.close()`, `do_teardown_appcontext`, resets the ContextVar, sends `appcontext_popped`, and finally re-raises collected errors as a `BaseExceptionGroup` on Python 3.11+.

Error path: `handle_exception` sends `got_request_exception`, re-raises when `PROPAGATE_EXCEPTIONS` (defaulting to `testing or debug`) is truthy, otherwise logs, wraps in `InternalServerError(original_exception=e)`, looks up a 500 handler, and finalizes with `from_error_handler=True` so response-processing failures are logged rather than raised.

Error handler lookup in `_find_error_handler` tries (specific code, then None) × (each blueprint name, then None), walking `exc_class.__mro__` at each step — so a blueprint handler for a specific code beats an app handler for that code, which beats class-based handlers.
CLI: `FlaskGroup.make_context` sets `os.environ["FLASK_RUN_FROM_CLI"] = "true"` so a stray module-level `app.run()` becomes a no-op that prints a red warning instead of blocking the command.
