qaReadiness.summary: Repo does not expose enough local browser QA structure for a reliable Synthetic QA workflow yet.

readmePreview: Requests Requests is a simple, yet elegant, HTTP library.

overview.summary: Requests is the PSF-maintained Python HTTP client library (`v2.34.2`, `src/requests/__version__.py`) that wraps urllib3 in a human-friendly API: `requests.get(...)` returns a `Response` with `.text`, `.json()`, `.cookies`, and `.raise_for_status()`. It is a pure-library distribution — no CLI, no server, no database — whose entire user surface is the seven module-level verb functions in `api.py` plus the `Session` object that persists cookies, auth, proxies, and a urllib3 connection pool across calls. What is distinctive in this commit is how much of the codebase is now type-machinery and hardening rather than new features: a private `_types.py` with `TypedDict` kwargs unpacking, pyright in `strict` mode over `src/requests/`, a pinned/hash-locked GitHub Actions setup audited by zizmor, and an explicit anti-LLM contribution policy. The architecture is deliberately layered so that the transport is swappable: `Session.mount(prefix, adapter)` is the single extension seam that every custom TLS, retry, or mock-transport integration in the ecosystem hangs off.

system_map.summary: There is no application entrypoint — the package root `src/requests/__init__.py` is the runtime boundary, and it does dependency-compatibility checking, optional pyOpenSSL SNI injection, and re-export of the public API before anything else runs. Beneath it sit four layers: the stateless verb wrappers (`api.py`), the stateful `Session` (`sessions.py`), the request/response value objects (`models.py`), and the urllib3-backed transport (`adapters.py`). Cross-cutting support lives in `utils.py` (proxies, netrc, header validation, length probing), `cookies.py` (a `CookieJar`/`MutableMapping` hybrid), `structures.py` (`CaseInsensitiveDict`, `LookupDict`), and `exceptions.py`. There is no storage layer: the only persistent state is the in-memory `RequestsCookieJar` on a `Session` and urllib3's connection pools. Build is setuptools via `pyproject.toml`; test/lint/typecheck/publish are four separate GitHub Actions workflows, and distribution is a Trusted-Publishing PyPI upload on `v*` tags.

claims.claim: The package root is the de-facto entrypoint: importing `requests` runs `check_compatibility()` to assert urllib3 >= 1.21.1 and chardet 3.0.2–8.0.0 / charset_normalizer 2.0.0–4.0.0, emitting `RequestsDependencyWarning` on mismatch rather than failing the import.

Import also attempts `pyopenssl.inject_into_urllib3()` when `ssl.HAS_SNI` is falsy and then version-checks `cryptography` via `_check_cryptography()`, warning if below 1.3.4 — a side effect that mutates urllib3 globally at import time.

The public API surface is fixed by the `__all__` tuple in `__init__.py`: 7 verb functions (`get/post/put/patch/delete/head/options`) plus `request`, the `Session`/`Request`/`PreparedRequest`/`Response` types, `codes`, and 9 exception classes.

`api.request()` is stateless by construction — it opens `sessions.Session()` in a `with` block for every call specifically to close sockets and avoid `ResourceWarning`, meaning module-level calls get zero connection reuse.

`Session.__init__` establishes all mutable session state (headers from `default_headers()`, empty proxies/params/hooks, `verify=True`, `max_redirects=DEFAULT_REDIRECT_LIMIT` of 30, `trust_env=True`) and mounts an `HTTPAdapter` for both `https://` and `http://`.

The transport boundary is `HTTPAdapter.send()`, which calls `conn.urlopen(..., redirect=False, preload_content=False, decode_content=False, retries=self.max_retries)` — requests deliberately disables urllib3's own redirect and decode handling and reimplements both.

The only external integrations are the four hard runtime dependencies declared in `pyproject.toml`: `charset_normalizer>=2,<4`, `idna>=2.5,<4`, `urllib3>=1.26,<3`, `certifi>=2023.5.7`; SOCKS and chardet are optional extras.

The CA bundle boundary is `certs.where()`, a one-line re-export of `certifi.where` that the module docstring explicitly names as the seam distro packagers should patch; it is captured once at import into `utils.DEFAULT_CA_BUNDLE_PATH`.

Build/test commands live in the `Makefile`: `make init` installs `requirements-dev.txt`, `make test` runs `pytest tests`, `make ci` adds `--junitxml=report.xml`, and `make coverage` runs pytest-cov against `src/requests`.

pytest is configured with `addopts = "--doctest-modules"` and `testpaths = ["tests"]`, so the docstring examples in `api.py`, `sessions.py`, and `status_codes.py` are executed as tests alongside the suite.

Deployment is PyPI-only via `.github/workflows/publish.yml`, which builds with `SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH` pinned to the commit time for reproducibility and publishes through `pypa/gh-action-pypi-publish` with `attestations: true` and `id-token: write` (Trusted Publishing, no stored API token).

Five CI workflows gate the repo: `run-tests.yml` (matrix of Python 3.10–3.15-dev plus 3.14t free-threaded and pypy-3.11, across ubuntu/macOS/windows), `lint.yml` (pre-commit), `typecheck.yml` (pyright), `codeql-analysis.yml`, and `zizmor.yml` for Actions-security scanning.

feature_catalog.summary: Every user-facing feature is a Python API, not a route or command. The catalog splits into: the seven HTTP verb helpers and their `Session` methods; request-construction features (params, form/JSON/multipart/streamed bodies, file uploads, IDNA hostnames); response-consumption features (`.text` with charset auto-detection, `.json()` with UTF-BOM sniffing, `.iter_content`/`.iter_lines` streaming, `.links` header parsing, `.raise_for_status`); and connection features (pooling, redirects, cookie persistence, proxy resolution including SOCKS, TLS verification and mTLS client certs, netrc auth, digest auth). Two auxiliary surfaces exist: `python -m requests.help` prints a JSON environment report for bug filing, and `python -m requests.certs` prints the CA bundle path.

claims.claim: Seven verb helpers are exposed at module level and mirrored as `Session` methods; `head()` uniquely defaults `allow_redirects` to `False` at both levels while `get`/`options` default it to `True`.

Request bodies support four distinct shapes decided in `prepare_body`: JSON via `complexjson.dumps(json, allow_nan=False)` → `application/json`; multipart via `_encode_files`; form-encoding via `_encode_params` → `application/x-www-form-urlencoded`; and streamed iterables/file objects that set `Transfer-Encoding: chunked` when length is unknown.
Multipart uploads accept 2-, 3-, and 4-tuples (`filename, fileobj`, `+content_type`, `+custom_headers`) and are assembled into urllib3 `RequestField` objects by `encode_multipart_formdata`.
Streaming bodies and file uploads are mutually exclusive — combining them raises `NotImplementedError("Streamed bodies and files are mutually exclusive.")`.

Internationalised domains are supported by `_get_idna_encoded_host()`, which applies `idna.encode(host, uts46=True)` for any non-ASCII host and raises `InvalidURL("URL has an invalid label.")` on failure.

`Response.text` decodes using the header-declared charset, falling back to `apparent_encoding` (charset_normalizer or chardet), and finally to `utf-8` with `errors="replace"` if no detection library is installed.
`Response.json()` sniffs UTF-8/16/32 via `guess_json_utf()` when no encoding is declared and the body exceeds 3 bytes, and normalises every decode failure into `requests.exceptions.JSONDecodeError`.

Streaming download is offered by `iter_content(chunk_size, decode_unicode)` and the line-oriented `iter_lines(delimiter=...)`; re-iterating a consumed non-streamed response raises `StreamConsumedError`.
Pagination via RFC 5988 is supported by `Response.links`, which parses the `Link` header through `parse_header_links()` and keys results by `rel` (falling back to `url`).

`requests.codes` is a `LookupDict` supporting attribute and item access with multiple aliases per code — including the joke aliases `codes['\\o/']` and `codes['✓']` for 200 — generated by `_init()` which also appends the full table to the module docstring.
Three auth handlers ship: `HTTPBasicAuth`, `HTTPProxyAuth` (same header under `Proxy-Authorization`), and `HTTPDigestAuth` supporting MD5, MD5-SESS, SHA, SHA-256 and SHA-512 with `qop=auth`.
`.netrc` credentials are honoured automatically when `trust_env` is true, checked at `$NETRC` if set otherwise `~/.netrc` and `~/_netrc`, and re-applied on cross-host redirects by `rebuild_auth`.

data_flow.summary: Input arrives as loosely-typed Python kwargs at `api.request()` or `Session.request()`, is funnelled into a `Request` value object, then normalised into a fully-serialised `PreparedRequest` (bytes body, `CaseInsensitiveDict` headers, percent-encoded URL string) by `Session.prepare_request()`. Session-level and environment-level settings are merged in at two distinct points — `merge_setting`/`merge_hooks` during preparation, and `merge_environment_settings` for proxies/verify/cert/stream just before send. The `PreparedRequest` crosses the adapter boundary into urllib3, and the urllib3 response crosses back through `HTTPAdapter.build_response()`, which is the sole constructor of `Response` objects. State ownership is clean: `Session` owns cookies, adapters and defaults; `PreparedRequest` owns the wire representation; `Response` owns `_content`/`_content_consumed` and lazily pulls bytes off `raw`. Output boundaries are the `Response` accessors and the environment mutations in `should_bypass_proxies` (via `set_environ`) and `extract_zipped_paths` (via `tempfile.mkstemp`).

claims.claim: Settings precedence is implemented by `merge_setting(request_setting, session_setting)`: non-Mapping request values win outright, Mappings are merged with request keys overriding, and any key explicitly set to `None` is deleted from the merged result — that is how callers suppress a session default header.
Hooks need special merging because `{'response': []}` would otherwise wipe session hooks; `merge_hooks` short-circuits when either side has an empty response list.

Cookies flow through a three-way merge in `prepare_request`: `merge_cookies(merge_cookies(RequestsCookieJar(), self.cookies), request.cookies)`, so per-request cookies layer over session cookies into a fresh jar rather than mutating the session's.

`PreparedRequest.prepare()` runs a fixed six-step pipeline — method, url, headers, cookies, body, auth — then hooks; the ordering comment states auth must be last so schemes like OAuth can sign a fully-formed request and still register hooks.

`prepare_auth` mutates the prepared request by `self.__dict__.update(r.__dict__)` from whatever the auth callable returns, then recomputes Content-Length — so an auth handler can legitimately rewrite body and headers.

Credentials embedded in the URL are extracted into auth during preparation: `prepare_auth` calls `get_auth_from_url(self.url)` when no explicit auth was supplied, and `prepare_url` reassembles netloc with the `auth@` prefix preserved.

Environment enters the flow at `merge_environment_settings`, which (only when `trust_env`) seeds proxies from `getproxies()` and overrides `verify` from `REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE` or `CURL_CA_BUNDLE` — explicitly to be cURL-compatible.

Proxy selection is layered: `resolve_proxies` consults `should_bypass_proxies` (NO_PROXY, CIDR matching, platform `proxy_bypass`), then `select_proxy` picks by the key precedence `scheme://host` → `scheme` → `all://host` → `all`.

Body length determination flows through `super_len()`, which probes `__len__`, `.len`, `fileno()`+`os.fstat`, and `seek/tell`, subtracting the current file position so partially-read files report the remaining bytes.
Header values are validated at the input boundary by `check_header_validity`, which regex-matches against `HEADER_VALIDATORS` to reject CR/LF and leading-whitespace — the CRLF-injection guard.

The response side is constructed exclusively in `HTTPAdapter.build_response()`, which lifts status, `CaseInsensitiveDict` headers, encoding from `get_encoding_from_headers`, `raw`, reason, url, extracts server cookies into `response.cookies`, and back-links `request` and `connection`.
Cookies persist onto the Session after the fact: `Session.send` calls `extract_cookies_to_jar(self.cookies, request, r.raw)` for the final response and separately for every entry in `r.history`.

behavior_traces.summary: Three flows carry most of the library's behaviour: the one-shot `requests.get()` path, the redirect-following loop inside `Session.send`, and the digest-auth 401 retry. All three converge on `Session.send` → `HTTPAdapter.send` → `build_response`. The redirect loop is a generator (`resolve_redirects`) that is fully drained inside `send`, which is why history arrives pre-assembled on the returned `Response`. The digest flow is unusual in that it re-enters the transport from a response hook (`r.connection.send(prep)`), bypassing `Session.send` entirely.

claims.claim: Import trace: `requests/__init__.py` runs `check_compatibility` → optional `pyopenssl.inject_into_urllib3` → `warnings.simplefilter('ignore', DependencyWarning)` → re-exports → `logging.getLogger(__name__).addHandler(NullHandler())` → `simplefilter('default', FileModeWarning, append=True)`.

One-shot GET trace: `api.get()` → `api.request()` opens `Session()` in a `with` → `Session.request()` → builds `Request` → `Session.prepare_request()` → `merge_environment_settings()` → `Session.send()` → returns, and `__exit__` calls `Session.close()` closing every adapter.

Preparation trace: `prepare_request` → `PreparedRequest.prepare()` → `prepare_method` (uppercases) → `prepare_url` (IDNA + `requote_uri(urlunparse(...))`) → `prepare_headers` (`check_header_validity` per header) → `prepare_cookies` (sets `Cookie` header once) → `prepare_body` → `prepare_auth` → `prepare_hooks`.

Send trace: `Session.send` defaults stream/verify/cert, rejects a bare `Request` with `ValueError("You can only send PreparedRequests.")`, resolves the adapter by longest matching prefix via `get_adapter`, times the call with `preferred_clock` into `r.elapsed`, then dispatches the `response` hook.

Adapter trace: `HTTPAdapter.send` → `get_connection_with_tls_context` → `cert_verify` (sets `conn.ca_certs`/`cert_file`, raising `OSError` if any path is missing) → `request_url` (full URL for proxied HTTP, path-only otherwise) → `add_headers` (no-op hook) → `conn.urlopen(...)` → `build_response`.

Redirect trace: `Session.send` calls `resolve_redirects(r, request)` and drains the generator into `history`; the generator per hop consumes `resp.content`, checks `len(resp.history) >= self.max_redirects` raising `TooManyRedirects`, calls `resp.close()`, normalises the Location, and copies the request.

On a non-307/308 redirect the loop strips `Content-Length`, `Content-Type` and `Transfer-Encoding` and blanks `prepared_request.body`, then always pops the `Cookie` header before re-deriving it from the jar.
Method rewriting per hop is `rebuild_method`: 303 → GET (unless HEAD), 302 → GET (unless HEAD, 'what browsers do, despite standards'), and 301 on a POST → GET.

Auth rewriting per hop is `rebuild_auth` → `should_strip_auth`, which drops `Authorization` on any hostname change but deliberately preserves it for http:80 → https:443 on the same host for backwards compatibility.

Body rewind trace: a redirect with `_body_position` set and a length header triggers `rewind_body(prepared_request)`; a prior failed `tell()` stores a sentinel `object()` so the rewind raises `UnrewindableBodyError` instead of hanging the connection.

Non-following trace: when `allow_redirects=False`, `Session.send` primes `r._next` by taking one item from `resolve_redirects(..., yield_requests=True)` inside a `try/except StopIteration`, which is what backs `Response.next`.

Digest trace: `HTTPDigestAuth.__call__` registers `handle_401` and `handle_redirect` as response hooks and records `r.body.tell()`; on a 4xx `handle_401` parses `www-authenticate`, consumes and closes the response, copies the request, builds the `Authorization` header and re-sends via `r.connection.send(prep, **kwargs)`, appending the original to `_r.history`.

testing_signals.summary: Testing is pytest-only, concentrated in one 108 KB file: `tests/test_requests.py` holds 237 of the ~347 test functions, with `tests/test_utils.py` (64) and `tests/test_lowlevel.py` (13) next. Integration tests run against a real local `httpbin` via the `pytest-httpbin` fixture (wrapped by `conftest.prepare_url` to guarantee a trailing slash), while wire-level behaviour uses a hand-rolled socket `Server` thread in `tests/testserver/server.py`. TLS behaviour is covered by checked-in fixture certificates (`tests/certs/{valid,expired,mtls}`) plus a `trustme`-generated no-SAN server fixture. Doctests in the library modules are executed by `--doctest-modules`. Gaps: `adapters.py` — the single most security-relevant module — has a one-test dedicated file, and there is no coverage threshold enforced anywhere.

claims.claim: The framework is pytest with `minversion = 6.2`, `testpaths = ["tests"]`, and `--doctest-modules` plus `NORMALIZE_WHITESPACE ELLIPSIS` optionflags, so module docstring examples are part of the suite.

Test distribution is extremely lopsided: `tests/test_requests.py` defines 237 `test_` functions across 7 classes (`TestRequests`, `TestCaseInsensitiveDict`, `TestMorselToCookieExpires`, `TestMorselToCookieMaxAge`, `TestTimeout`, `RedirectSession`, `TestPreparingURLs`), versus 64 in `test_utils.py` and 13 in `test_lowlevel.py`.

An autouse fixture `clean_proxy_environ` monkeypatches away `http_proxy`, `https_proxy`, `no_proxy`, `ftp_proxy` and `all_proxy` (both cases) for every test, so proxy tests must set env vars explicitly.
Integration coverage runs against a live httpbin server through the `httpbin`/`httpbin_secure` fixtures, pinned via `pytest-httpbin==2.1.0` and `httpbin~=0.10.0` in the `test` dependency group.

Wire-level tests use a purpose-built threaded socket server with `text_response_server` / `basic_response_server` helpers, exercising chunked upload, conflicting Content-Length, RFC 1808 non-ASCII redirects and fragment handling.
Digest auth is covered at the socket level by three dedicated tests: `test_digestauth_401_count_reset_on_redirect`, `test_digestauth_401_only_sent_once`, and `test_digestauth_only_on_4xx`.

TLS paths are tested with committed fixture certs — expired server cert, valid server cert, and an mTLS client cert — including `test_different_connection_pool_for_mtls_settings` verifying pool-key separation.
A `nosan_server` fixture mints a CA and a commonName-only (no subjectAltName) certificate at runtime using `trustme`, backing the SNI/SAN warning tests.
`test_response_iter_lines_reentrant` is marked `@pytest.mark.xfail` and documents a known defect: `Response.iter_lines()` is not reentrant-safe, matching the docstring note on the method itself.

Behaviour differences between urllib3 1.x and 2.x are handled by skips keyed on `is_urllib3_1`, e.g. `test_content_length_for_string_data_counts_bytes` skips on 1.x because it encodes strings as latin-1 rather than utf-8.
`adapters.py` has a single dedicated regression test (`test_request_url_handles_leading_path_separators`); the rest of the adapter is exercised only indirectly through `test_requests.py`.
CI runs `make ci` (`pytest tests --junitxml=report.xml`) across 8 Python versions × 3 OSes, plus two special jobs: `no_chardet` uninstalls both detection libraries, and `urllib3` pins `urllib3<2`.

risk_map.summary: As a library in ~4M dependent repos, the blast radius of any change here is close to maximal, and the highest-risk surfaces are the ones that decide whether credentials cross a trust boundary: `should_strip_auth`, `rebuild_proxies`, `prepare_url`, and `cert_verify`. Several behaviours are knowingly non-ideal and preserved for backwards compatibility — the http→https auth-retention carve-out, `_basic_auth_str` accepting non-strings, and `LookupDict.__getitem__` silently returning `None`. Environment trust is on by default (`trust_env=True`), so `.netrc`, `$NETRC`, `REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE`/`CURL_CA_BUNDLE` and `*_proxy` variables all influence behaviour implicitly. Filesystem and process-global side effects exist in `extract_zipped_paths`, `atomic_open`, `set_environ`, and the import-time `pyopenssl.inject_into_urllib3()`.

claims.claim: `should_strip_auth` intentionally keeps the `Authorization` header across an http:80 → https:443 redirect on the same host; the comment states this is not RFC 7235 behaviour and is retained only for backwards compatibility.

`rebuild_proxies` reconstructs `Proxy-Authorization` from proxy URL credentials but skips it when the target scheme starts with `https`, explicitly to avoid leaking the header into a TLS tunnel — a subtle invariant easy to break in a refactor.

Any URL containing a colon whose scheme does not start with `http` bypasses all URL preparation and is assigned verbatim to `self.url`, so `mailto:`/`data:`-style inputs skip IDNA, requoting and host validation entirely.

`verify=False` disables certificate and hostname validation at the urllib3 level (`cert_reqs = 'CERT_NONE'`, ca_certs cleared); the Session docstring is explicit that this exposes callers to MitM and is for testing only.
`trust_env=True` by default means an attacker-controlled or accidentally-set `REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE`/`CURL_CA_BUNDLE` silently replaces the trust store for every request on the session.

`get_netrc_auth` reads credentials from a path taken from the `$NETRC` environment variable without restriction, and swallows `NetrcParseError`/`OSError` unless `raise_errors=True` — failures to read credentials are silent by default.

`extract_zipped_paths` performs file IO outside the repo root: it walks a path upward looking for a zip archive, then extracts a member into a `tempfile.mkstemp()` file that is never cleaned up, returning that path to the caller.

`_basic_auth_str` still accepts non-string usernames/passwords, coercing them with a `DeprecationWarning` promising removal in 3.0.0; the source comment preserves it precisely because callers depend on it.

Digest auth uses MD5 by default when the server omits an `algorithm` directive; MD5/SHA-1 usage is flagged `usedforsecurity=False` to appease FIPS builds but the weak-hash negotiation is server-driven.

`handle_401` re-sends the authenticated request directly through `r.connection.send(prep, **kwargs)`, bypassing `Session.send` — so session-level cookie extraction, hooks, and redirect resolution do not run for that hop.

`prepare_auth` blanket-applies `self.__dict__.update(r.__dict__)` from a user-supplied callable, meaning a third-party auth class can overwrite any attribute of the PreparedRequest including `url` and `hooks`.
`LookupDict.__getitem__` deliberately falls through to `None` for unknown keys, so a typo'd `requests.codes['okey']` silently yields `None` instead of raising — a footgun with no test-enforced guard.

extension_points.summary: There is one primary extension seam and several secondary ones. The primary is the Transport Adapter: `Session.mount(prefix, adapter)` keeps `self.adapters` sorted by descending prefix length and `get_adapter` picks the longest matching prefix, so any URL prefix can be routed to a `BaseAdapter` subclass — this is how retry policies, custom TLS contexts, and test doubles are injected. Secondary seams are the response hook system, the `AuthBase` callable protocol, the `SessionRedirectMixin` methods documented as overridable, and the packager-facing `certs.where()`. Nearly every private-looking `HTTPAdapter` method carries a docstring saying it exists specifically for subclass overrides.

claims.claim: `Session.mount(prefix, adapter)` is the registry: it inserts into the `self.adapters` OrderedDict then re-pops every shorter key so adapters stay in descending prefix-length order.

`Session.get_adapter(url)` resolves by case-insensitive `startswith` over that ordered map, raising `InvalidSchema(f"No connection adapters were found for {url!r}")` when nothing matches — so registering a new scheme is purely a mount call.
`BaseAdapter` defines the minimal contract — `send(request, stream, timeout, verify, cert, proxies)` and `close()` — that any replacement transport must implement.

Eight `HTTPAdapter` methods are documented as subclass-override points rather than user API: `init_poolmanager`, `proxy_manager_for`, `cert_verify`, `build_response`, `get_connection_with_tls_context`, `request_url`, `add_headers`, and `proxy_headers`.

`HTTPAdapter.add_headers()` is an intentional empty hook — 'As of v2.0 this does nothing by default, but is left for overriding by users that subclass' — and is called on every send with the full kwargs.
`init_poolmanager(**pool_kwargs)` forwards arbitrary kwargs to `urllib3.PoolManager`, which is the documented way to inject a custom `ssl_context` or TLS version.

The hook registry is the `HOOKS = ['response']` list in `hooks.py`, with `default_hooks()` building `{event: []}` and `dispatch_hook()` chaining callables so each non-None return replaces the data for the next hook.

Hooks can be attached per-request (`hooks=` kwarg), per-session (`Session.hooks`), or programmatically via `RequestHooksMixin.register_hook` / `deregister_hook`, which both `Request` and `PreparedRequest` inherit.
Custom auth plugs in via `AuthBase`, whose `__call__(self, r) -> PreparedRequest` raises `NotImplementedError` by default; `prepare_auth` treats any non-2-tuple auth value as such a callable.

`SessionRedirectMixin` is a separately-inheritable class exposing `get_redirect_target`, `should_strip_auth`, `resolve_redirects`, `rebuild_auth`, `rebuild_proxies` and `rebuild_method` — the tests subclass it directly as `RedirectSession` to exercise redirect logic without a network.
`get_redirect_target`'s docstring explicitly invites a custom mixin that caches the redirect location on the response as a private attribute, acknowledging the method is called redundantly per hop.
`certs.where()` is the packager extension point: the module docstring instructs distributors to change its definition to return a separately packaged CA bundle.

agent_handoff.summary: Treat this repo as a stability-first, extremely high-blast-radius library: the maintainers protect version, changelog, workflows and pyproject behind CODEOWNERS, and the project has a written policy banning unsupervised agentic contributions. Read `sessions.py`, `models.py` and `adapters.py` before touching anything; almost every non-obvious branch in them encodes a specific GitHub issue number that you should look up before 'simplifying' it. Local loop is `make init` then `make test`; before pushing, run `pre-commit run --all-files` and `pyright src/requests/`, since lint and typecheck are separate required CI gates. The biggest trap is that `tests/` is excluded from pyright but `src/requests/` is checked in `strict` mode, so type annotations in library code must be complete and the codebase is dense with deliberate `# type: ignore` comments carrying explanatory reasons — preserve them.

claims.claim: `.github/AI_POLICY.md` states 'Absolutely no unsupervised agentic tools' and requires a human copyright owner per contribution with no LLM bots in `Co-authored-by:` — do not open PRs against this upstream without explicit human sponsorship.

Read first, in order: `src/requests/api.py` (surface), `src/requests/sessions.py` (orchestration), `src/requests/models.py` (value objects), `src/requests/adapters.py` (transport). These four contain the whole request lifecycle.
Local setup and test: `make init` installs `requirements-dev.txt` (editable `.[socks]`, pytest, pytest-httpbin, httpbin, trustme); `make test` runs `pytest tests`; `make ci` matches CI exactly.
Two additional gates must pass before merge: `pre-commit run --all-files` (ruff-check --fix and ruff-format) and `python -m pyright src/requests/` under `typeCheckingMode = "strict"`.

Style is enforced by ruff with rule sets E/W/F/I/UP/T10 targeting py310, ignoring E203/E501/UP031, with per-file `E402,F401` exemptions for `src/requests/__init__.py` and `src/requests/compat.py` — do not 'clean up' those unused imports, they are the public re-export surface.

`src/requests/_types.py` is explicitly documented as not part of the public API; it hosts the `RequestKwargs`/`GetKwargs`/`PostKwargs`/`DataKwargs` TypedDicts consumed via `Unpack` in `api.py` and `sessions.py`, so adding a request kwarg means editing both the runtime signature and the TypedDict.

`_types.is_prepared()` is a typing-only narrowing helper that returns `True` unconditionally at runtime; the many `assert _is_prepared(request)` lines are type assertions, not validation — do not convert them into runtime checks.

Safe edit boundary: new transport behaviour belongs in an `HTTPAdapter` subclass or the documented override methods, not in `Session.send`, because `Session.send` is also reached by `resolve_redirects` and any change there multiplies across every redirect hop.

Trap: `prepare_cookies` can only meaningfully run once per PreparedRequest — cookielib will not regenerate the header if `Cookie` already exists, which is why `resolve_redirects` pops the header before re-preparing.

Trap: branch comments cite issue numbers as the rationale (e.g. #1084 for the 307/308 carve-out, #3490 for the purged headers, #1704 for POST-301→GET, #3772 for digest-only-on-4xx, #5229 for the `fileno` AttributeError). Look these up before changing the branch.

Trap: `compat.py` rebinds `str` and `bytes` to the builtins and exports `basestring = (str, bytes)`; modules importing from it (`auth.py`, `utils.py`, `adapters.py`) rely on these shadows, so removing them is a wide breaking change.
Tests requiring network-like behaviour need the local httpbin fixture; use the `httpbin` fixture (which yields a URL-joining callable, not a string) rather than hardcoding `https://httpbin.org`.

name: ripgrep

health.summary: Deterministic scan scored 93 source files across simple size, churn, structural, test-adjacency, and performance-risk signals. 32 hotspots surfaced; average score is 7.1/10. Treat these as review leads, not proof of a bug.

qaReadiness.summary: Repo does not expose enough local browser QA structure for a reliable Synthetic QA workflow yet.

readmePreview: ripgrep (rg) ------------ ripgrep is a line-oriented search tool that recursively searches the current directory for a regex pattern.

overview.summary: ripgrep is a line-oriented recursive search tool (`rg`) written in Rust that walks a directory tree while respecting `.gitignore`/`.ignore` rules, matches each file with either Rust's `regex` crate or PCRE2, and prints results through one of three printers (standard/summary/JSON). The repository is a Cargo workspace: a thin binary crate at `crates/core` glues together ten reusable library crates (`grep-matcher`, `grep-regex`, `grep-pcre2`, `grep-searcher`, `grep-printer`, `grep-cli`, `ignore`, `globset`, plus the experimental `grep-index`), each published independently on crates.io. What is distinctive is the amount of engineering in the boring parts: a hand-rolled CLI parser over a 246KB table of `&dyn Flag` trait objects that also generates the man page, `--help` text and four shells' completions from the same source of truth; a directory walker that reimplements gitignore precedence with a parallel work-stealing traversal; and a searcher that chooses between memory maps, a reusable line buffer, and multi-line slice scanning per file. An unstable `unstable-index` feature adds a redb+fst ngram index behind `-X/--index` and `--x-crud`.

system_map.summary: The workspace root `Cargo.toml` declares the `ripgrep` package producing one binary `rg` from `crates/core/main.rs`, and lists ten workspace members under `crates/`. `crates/core` is not published as a library — it is pure glue plus the CLI definition, as its README states. Dependencies flow strictly downward: core → `grep` facade → `grep-searcher`/`grep-printer`/`grep-regex`/`grep-pcre2`/`grep-cli`/`grep-matcher`, with `ignore` and `globset` used for traversal and glob filtering. There is no network, database or server component in the default build; the only external integrations are subprocesses (decompressors, `--pre` preprocessor, hostname binary) and, under `unstable-index`, a redb embedded database on disk. Deployment is static binaries cross-compiled for ~14 targets by a tag-triggered GitHub Actions release workflow, plus a Debian package described by `[package.metadata.deb]`.

claims.claim: The single binary target `rg` is declared in the root manifest with `path = "crates/core/main.rs"`, and `autotests = false` with one explicit `[[test]] name = "integration", path = "tests/tests.rs"`.

`fn main() -> ExitCode` calls `run(flags::parse())` and dispatches on `args.mode()` into seven arms: indexed search, single-threaded `search`, `search_parallel`, `index::write`, `files`/`files_parallel`, `types`, and `generate`.

The workspace has ten members — `globset`, `grep`, `cli`, `index`, `matcher`, `pcre2`, `printer`, `regex`, `searcher`, `ignore` — sharing `edition = "2024"` and `rust-version = "1.96"` via `[workspace.package]`.
`crates/grep` is a pure facade that re-exports the constituent crates as `grep::cli`, `grep::matcher`, `grep::printer`, `grep::regex`, `grep::searcher` and (feature-gated) `grep::pcre2`.

The published crate names differ from directory names: `crates/matcher` is `grep-matcher` v0.1.9, `crates/printer` is `grep-printer` v0.3.1, `crates/searcher` is `grep-searcher` v0.1.17, `crates/regex` is `grep-regex` v0.1.14.

There is no persistent storage in the default build; the only storage layer is the optional `grep-index` crate, which opens a redb `Database`/`ReadOnlyDatabase` at a file named `index.db` inside a discovered `.ripgrep` directory.

`grep-index` is marked `publish = false`, version `0.0.1`, and is wired in only through the `unstable-index` Cargo feature (`dep:grep-index`), which the root manifest itself warns "may have very serious bugs".

Index code is compiled behind a `#[path]` module swap: `crates/core/index/mod.rs` selects `disabled.rs` (which `bail!`s "indexing not enabled in this build") or `enabled.rs` based on the `unstable-index` feature.

`build.rs` embeds the short git hash as `RIPGREP_BUILD_GIT_HASH` by shelling out to `git rev-parse --short=10 HEAD`, and on `windows`+`msvc` embeds `pkg/windows/Manifest.xml` via `/MANIFEST:EMBED` linker args to enable long paths.

Build/test commands are `cargo build --release` (optionally `--features pcre2`) and `cargo test --all`; CI additionally runs `cargo test --workspace --features unstable-index` and `cargo fmt --all --check`.
On musl 64-bit targets the binary swaps in jemalloc as the `#[global_allocator]` because musl's allocator measurably slows ripgrep down; this is the only allocator override.

Release shape: a `release-lto` profile (fat LTO, `panic = "abort"`, `codegen-units = 1`, symbols stripped) plus `.cargo/config.toml` forcing `+crt-static` for MSVC and musl targets so shipped binaries are statically linked.

feature_catalog.summary: ripgrep's user surface is a single command with a very large flag set: `FLAGS` in `crates/core/flags/defs.rs` is a static slice of `&dyn Flag` trait objects, each carrying short/long/negated/alias names, a documentation category, short and long (mdoc) help text, a completion type, and an `update` method that mutates `LowArgs`. Beyond plain search, the binary has distinct top-level modes — `--files`, `--type-list`, `--generate`, `-h/--help`/`-V/--version` special modes, and the experimental index modes. Output modes (`--count`, `--count-matches`, `-l/--files-with-matches`, `--files-without-match`, `--json`) select among three printers. Filtering features include gitignore semantics, `-t/--type` file types, `-g/--glob` overrides, hidden-file handling and `--max-filesize`. Provider-style integrations are the pluggable regex engine (`--engine auto|default|pcre2`), decompression (`-z`), arbitrary preprocessors (`--pre`), and terminal hyperlinks.

claims.claim: `Mode` enumerates the five top-level behaviors — `Search(SearchMode)`, `Index(IndexMode)`, `Files`, `Types`, `Generate(GenerateMode)` — with `Mode::Search(SearchMode::Standard)` as the default.

`SearchMode` has six variants (`Standard`, `FilesWithMatches`, `FilesWithoutMatch`, `Count`, `CountMatches`, `JSON`) and `HiArgs::printer` maps them onto `Printer::Standard`, `Printer::JSON` or `Printer::Summary` with a `SummaryKind`.

`--generate` emits ancillary artifacts: `GenerateMode::Man` produces roff, and `CompleteBash`/`CompleteZsh`/`CompleteFish`/`CompletePowerShell` produce shell completions, all rendered from the same `FLAGS` table.

`-h` and `--help` render different documents (`generate_short` vs `generate_long`) from `template.short.help` / `template.long.help`, interpolating per-category placeholders like `!!filter!!` and `!!output-modes!!`.
`--type-list` is implemented by `types()` in main, which iterates `args.types().definitions()` and prints `name: glob, glob` lines, exiting 1 if there are no definitions.
ripgrep ships a large built-in file-type table, `DEFAULT_TYPES`, mapping type names to glob lists (e.g. `ada` → `*.adb`,`*.ads`), extensible per-invocation via `--type-add`.

Three regex engine choices are supported: `EngineChoice::Default` (Rust regex), `PCRE2`, and `Auto`, where `Auto` tries Rust first and falls back to PCRE2, reporting both errors side by side if both fail.

`-z/--search-zip` transparently decompresses by file extension using external binaries: gzip, bzip2, xz (also for `.lzma`), lz4, brotli, zstd and `uncompress`, keyed by globs like `*.gz`, `*.tgz`, `*.zst`, `*.Z`.
`--pre` runs an arbitrary user program per file with the path as argv[1] and the file on stdin, optionally restricted by `--pre-glob` via `preprocessor_globs`.

Hyperlink support is a first-class feature with named aliases (e.g. `"vscode".parse::<HyperlinkFormat>()`) and interpolation variables including `{host}` and a `{wslprefix}` derived from `WSL_DISTRO_NAME`.

Sorting is user-selectable across four criteria — `path`, `modified`, `accessed`, `created` — with reverse variants; `HiArgs::sort` special-cases ascending path sort to be done during traversal instead of by buffering.

The experimental indexing surface consists of `--x-crud` (create/update/remove index entries), `--x-index-force` and `--x-index-path`, all in the `Category::Indexing` group, which renders as "Indexing is not supported in this build of ripgrep." when the feature is off.

data_flow.summary: Input enters at three boundaries: `std::env::args_os()`, an optional rc file named by `RIPGREP_CONFIG_PATH`, and stdin (patterns via `-f -`, or the haystack itself). The parser folds all of these into a flat, dumb `LowArgs` struct through `Flag::update`, then `HiArgs::from_low_args` performs all the "expensive" derivations — compiling globs, building the type matcher, resolving the CWD and hostname, choosing thread count and mmap strategy. `HiArgs` is the single state owner for the rest of the process; every downstream object (`ignore::WalkBuilder`, `grep::searcher::Searcher`, the matcher, the printer, the `SearchWorker`) is constructed from it by a dedicated accessor. Bytes then flow file → `Searcher` → `Sink` → printer → `termcolor` writer, either directly to stdout (single-threaded) or into per-thread `termcolor::Buffer`s flushed by a `BufferWriter` (parallel). Exit status is a fourth output channel, driven by a match flag plus a global `ERRORED` atomic.

claims.claim: Config args are read from the file named by `RIPGREP_CONFIG_PATH`, one shell argument per line with `#` comments and blank lines skipped, then **prepended** to `std::env::args_os().skip(1)` and the whole CLI is re-parsed from scratch.
`--no-config` short-circuits before the config file is read, and `-h`/`-V` short-circuit even earlier via `ParseResult::Special`, so help output never depends on the config file or the CWD.

Each flag writes into `LowArgs` — a flat struct of ~60 public(crate) fields — via `Flag::update(FlagValue, &mut LowArgs)`, and by convention `update` only validates, deferring side effects (e.g. resolving `--hostname-bin`) to the high-level stage.

Patterns are drained from `LowArgs` by `Patterns::from_low_args`, which promotes the first positional to a pattern only when neither `-e` nor `-f` was given, reads `-f -` through `grep::cli::patterns_from_stdin()`, and de-duplicates patterns to avoid pathological regex compile costs.

`Paths::from_low_args` runs after patterns so all remaining positionals are paths; with none given it uses `grep::cli::is_readable_stdin()` as a heuristic to choose between searching `./` and searching `-` (stdin), and errors if stdin would be consumed twice.
`State` tracks one-shot derived facts across the low→high conversion, notably `stdin_consumed`, which is what makes the double-stdin error and the CWD heuristic consistent.
Thread count is derived once in `from_low_args`: forced to 1 when `--sort` is set or only one file is searched, else `--threads`, else `available_parallelism()` capped at 12.
Memory-map policy is decided from the path set: `MmapMode::Auto` only enables mmap when ≤10 paths are given and all of them are files; otherwise `MmapChoice::never()`.

Traversal output is `Result<ignore::DirEntry, ignore::Error>`, converted by `HaystackBuilder::build_from_result` into `Option<Haystack>`; errors are reported through `err_message!` and non-file, non-explicit entries are dropped with a debug log.
`SearchWorker::search` selects among four data sources per haystack in priority order: stdin lock, preprocessor subprocess, decompression subprocess, then direct `search_path`.

Search results reach printers only through the `Sink` trait (`matched`, `context`, `context_break`, `binary_data`, `begin`, `finish`); `search_path`/`search_reader` build a `sink_with_path` per printer variant and harvest `has_match()` and `stats()` from it.

In parallel mode each worker owns a cloned `SearchWorker` writing into its own `termcolor::Buffer`; the buffer is cleared before each file and printed atomically via `bufwtr.print(...)` to avoid interleaving.

behavior_traces.summary: Three flows dominate: startup/arg-parsing, a default recursive search, and the file-listing path. All of them funnel through `flags::parse()` → `HiArgs` and then diverge on `Mode`. The parallel search path is notable because parallelism lives entirely in the directory walker — `search_parallel` just hands a closure to `WalkParallel::run` and never manages threads itself. The indexed path currently degrades gracefully: `index::read` opens the index and then falls straight through to the ordinary exhaustive search.

claims.claim: Startup order: `main` → `flags::parse()` → `parse_low()` which first calls `Logger::init()`, then `Parser::new().parse(env::args_os().skip(1), &mut low)`, then `set_log_levels(&low)` so `--trace` is live before config parsing.

If a config file yields arguments, the parser discards the first `LowArgs`, builds a fresh `LowArgs::default()`, re-parses `config_args ++ argv`, and re-runs `set_log_levels` because logging flags may have changed.

`Parser::new()` returns a `&'static Parser` memoized in a `OnceLock`, so the flag-name trie (`FlagMap` over short names, long names, aliases and negations) is built exactly once per process even though `lookup()` calls it repeatedly.
`HiArgs::from_low_args` begins by asserting `low.special == None` ("special mode demands short-circuiting"), which encodes the invariant that help/version never reach high-level conversion.

Default search trace: `run` → `search(args, mode)` → `args.walk_builder()?.build()` → `haystack_builder.build_from_result` → `args.sort(...)` → `args.search_worker(args.matcher()?, args.searcher()?, args.printer(mode, args.stdout()))` → loop `searcher.search(&haystack)`.

Inside one file's search: `SearchWorker::search` sets binary detection (explicit vs implicit) on the `Searcher`, then `search_path` dispatches on the `PatternMatcher` enum to the generic `search_path(m, searcher, printer, path)`, which calls `p.sink_with_path(&matcher, path)` and `searcher.search_path`.

`Searcher::search_path` → `search_file_maybe_path` first tries `self.config.mmap.open(file, path)` and searches the resulting slice; only if mmap is unavailable does it fall back to the incremental reader path.
The searcher has three internal strategies implemented in `glue.rs`: `ReadByLine` (streaming reader), `SliceByLine` (whole-slice, e.g. mmap) and `MultiLine` (when `--multiline` is on).

Parallel search trace: `search_parallel` creates a `BufferWriter`, an `AtomicBool` matched/searched pair and an optional `Mutex<Stats>`, then `args.walk_builder()?.build_parallel().run(|| Box::new(move |result| ...))` clones a `SearchWorker` per thread.

Early exit under `-q/--quiet` is implemented twice: the sequential loop `break`s when `matched && args.quit_after_match()`, and the parallel closure returns `WalkState::Quit`, which aborts the whole traversal.

Broken pipe is handled at three levels: inside the search loop (`break`), inside `bufwtr.print` (`WalkState::Quit`), and finally in `main`, which walks `err.chain()` for an `io::Error` of kind `BrokenPipe` and returns exit code 0.

Preprocessor trace: `search_preprocessor` builds `Command::new(bin).arg(path).stdin(Stdio::from(File::open(path)?))`, wraps it in a `CommandReader`, searches the reader, then calls `rdr.close()` so a non-zero exit code surfaces stderr as a Rust error.

testing_signals.summary: Testing is two-tier and unusually thorough for a CLI. Integration tests live in `tests/` behind a single `[[test]] integration` target and drive the real `rg` binary in a temp directory via a `Dir`/`TestCommand` harness; the `rgtest!` macro automatically runs every test twice — once with the default engine and once with PCRE2 — when the `pcre2` feature is on. Unit tests live inline in `#[cfg(test)] mod tests` blocks, heavily concentrated in `crates/core/flags/defs.rs` (116 `#[test]`s, mostly per-flag parse assertions) and `crates/printer/src/standard.rs` (74). CI runs the suite on 18 build configurations including cross-compiled big-endian (s390x, powerpc64) and 32-bit targets, plus rustfmt, `cargo doc` with `-D warnings`, a wasm32-wasip1 build check, and a cargo-fuzz compile check. There is no coverage measurement and no benchmark job; `benchsuite/` is a separate Python/shell harness not run by CI.

claims.claim: The integration suite is one binary: `tests/tests.rs` declares modules `binary`, `feature`, `json`, `misc`, `multiline`, `regression`, plus `index` gated on `#[cfg(feature = "unstable-index")]`.
Test volume by area: `regression.rs` has 110 `rgtest!` cases, `misc.rs` 95, `feature.rs` 82, `binary.rs` 29, `json.rs` 9, `multiline.rs` 8 — regression tests are the single largest group.

`rgtest!` runs each test body twice when built with the `pcre2` feature — once via `util::setup` and once via `util::setup_pcre2` — which is why CI skips PCRE2 tests under cross/qemu to avoid doubling runtime.
`Dir::new` locates the `rg` binary relative to `env::current_exe()` and creates an isolated temp working directory keyed by a global atomic counter, so tests can create real files and symlinks.
`TestCommand::env` exists specifically so tests can exercise environment-driven behavior such as `RIPGREP_CONFIG_PATH`.
Decompression is covered by committed fixture files: `tests/data/` contains `sherlock.{gz,bz2,xz,lz4,lzma,br,zst,Z}` matching the glob table in `default_decompression_commands`.
`cmd_exists` lets tests skip gracefully when an external decompression binary isn't installed on the runner, by probing `program --help`.

Index tests are split into `tests/index/basic.rs` (UX happy paths) and `tests/index/disallowed.rs`, the latter asserting that `-X` combined with `--files-without-match`, `--text` or `-Eutf16` errors out.
`crates/core/flags/defs.rs` carries 116 `#[test]` functions — largely `parse_low_raw([...])` assertions per flag — making the flag table the most densely unit-tested file in the repo.

Structural invariants of the flag table are enforced by tests: `shorts_no_duplicates`, `longs_no_duplicates`, `shorts_all_ascii_alphanumeric` and `longs_all_ascii_alphanumeric` (which also validates aliases and negations).
CI runs two informational tests with `--nocapture`: `flags::defs::tests::available_shorts` (prints unused short-flag letters) and grep-cli's `print_hostname`.
Shell completion correctness is tested outside cargo by the `ci/test-complete` script, which is skipped on Windows and on cross-compiled targets.

risk_map.summary: ripgrep has a small but real attack surface for a search tool: it executes external programs (decompressors, `--pre`, `--hostname-bin`), reads a config file from an environment-variable-named path whose contents become command-line flags, and memory-maps files it does not control. The codebase acknowledges most of these explicitly in comments — the mmap `unsafe` block calls its own reasoning "suspect", and `resolve_binary` exists specifically to stop Windows CWD-relative program resolution. The most fragile coupling is the 246KB `defs.rs` flag table, where a single flag touches parsing, help text, man page and four completion generators. The experimental index path is the least-finished area: `grep-index` opens with `#![allow(warnings)]`, its literal module is self-described as a prototype, and `index::read` doesn't actually use the index yet.

claims.claim: Arbitrary code execution is by design in three places — `--pre` (`Command::new(bin).arg(path)`), `-z` decompressors, and `--hostname-bin` — all spawned with the user's environment inherited.

`resolve_binary` is a deliberate Windows security mitigation: without it, `Command::new` hands relative paths to `CreateProcess`, which searches the CWD, so `rg -z` in an untrusted tree could run an attacker-planted `gzip.exe`. On non-Windows it is a no-op returning the path unchanged.

`RIPGREP_CONFIG_PATH` turns a file's contents into command-line arguments that are prepended to argv, so anything that can set that env var or write that file can inject flags including `--pre` — a full code-execution vector with no allowlist or validation.

The memory-map `unsafe` block carries an explicit hazard note: a file truncated concurrently with the search can raise SIGBUS and abort the process, and the author writes "This reasoning should be treated as suspect."

File IO is unbounded outside the repo root by nature — `walk_builder` starts at user-supplied paths with `follow_links(self.follow)` and `same_file_system(self.one_file_system)`, so `-L` on a hostile tree can be walked out of the intended subtree.
Index discovery reads `RIPGREP_INDEX_PATH` and otherwise walks every ancestor of the CWD looking for `.ripgrep`, a lookup the code itself flags as "subject to TOCTOU problems".
`crates/index/src/lib.rs` opens with `#![allow(warnings)]`, suppressing all compiler lints for the entire index crate — including dead code and unused results.

`crates/index/src/literal.rs` is self-described as "currently a prototype ... hastily written in order to bootstrap ngram extraction", so the ngram query construction (`GramQuery::And/Or/Literal`) is not production-hardened.
Indexed search is effectively dead weight today: `index::read` binds the opened index to `let _index` and runs a full exhaustive search anyway, so `-X` costs index-open time for zero pruning benefit.

`crates/core/flags/defs.rs` is 246KB — larger than the next two biggest files combined — and each flag must stay consistent across `Flag::update`, `doc_short`, `doc_long`, `doc_category` and `completion_type`, making it the highest blast-radius file for CLI changes.

`FlagValue::unwrap_switch`/`unwrap_value` panic via `unreachable!` on mismatch; this is intentional (a bug indicator) but means an `is_switch()`/`update()` inconsistency in a new flag is a runtime panic rather than a compile error.

Error reporting is global mutable state: three `AtomicBool`s (`MESSAGES`, `IGNORE_MESSAGES`, `ERRORED`) set once at startup and read at exit, so any code path that prints an error without going through `err_message!` silently fails to change the exit code.

extension_points.summary: ripgrep's extension seams are almost all static tables and traits rather than runtime plugin systems. Adding a flag means adding one unit struct implementing `Flag` and one entry in the `FLAGS` slice; everything downstream (parser trie, `-h`, `--help`, man page, four shell completions) derives from that. Adding a file type means one line in `DEFAULT_TYPES`. Adding a decompressor means one `add(glob, ARGS, &mut cmds)` line. At the library level, `Matcher` and `Sink` are the two real trait-based extension points: any regex engine implementing `grep_matcher::Matcher` can be plugged into the searcher, and any output format implementing `grep_searcher::Sink` can consume results. The `ParallelVisitorBuilder` trait in `ignore` lets external callers drive the parallel walker with their own per-thread state.

claims.claim: The primary extension point is the `Flag` trait plus the `FLAGS: &[&dyn Flag]` slice; the module doc states the `defs` module "provides a single global slice of `&dyn Flag` values corresponding to all of the flags in ripgrep" used via dynamic dispatch.
One `Flag` impl can expose four user-visible names — short, long, `name_negated()` and an arbitrary `aliases()` list — as with `-E`/`--encoding`/`--no-encoding` sharing a single implementation.

`Category` (Input, Search, Filter, Output, OutputModes, Indexing, Logging, OtherBehaviors) is the grouping key for generated docs; `Category::as_str` returns the template variable name interpolated into help and man templates.
`CompletionType` (Other, Filename, Executable, Filetype, Encoding) is the hook a new flag uses to tell all four shell completion generators what to complete.

Four completion generators are registered in `flags::mod` as `generate_complete_bash/zsh/fish/powershell` and surfaced through `GenerateMode`; adding a shell means adding a module under `flags/complete/` and a `GenerateMode` variant.

`grep_searcher::Sink` is the output extension trait — implement `matched`, `context`, `context_break`, `binary_data`, `begin`, `finish` — and the crate ships a `sinks` submodule of closure-based conveniences (e.g. `UTF8`) for quick use.
`grep_matcher::Matcher` is the regex-engine extension trait; `grep-regex` and `grep-pcre2` are two implementations, and `PatternMatcher` in core is the enum that selects between them at runtime.

Printers are extended by adding a `Printer<W>` enum variant plus a `printer_*` builder in `HiArgs`; each variant only needs `get_mut()` and a `sink_with_path` method for `search_path`/`search_reader` to work.

New file types plug into `DEFAULT_TYPES`, a `&[(&[&str], &[&str])]` table of (names, globs) that the doc comment explicitly invites PRs against; users extend it per-invocation with `TypesBuilder::add`/`add_def`.

New decompressors plug into `default_decompression_commands()` via a single `add(glob, ARGS_X, &mut cmds)` call; unavailable binaries are silently skipped after `resolve_binary` fails with a debug log.
`ignore::ParallelVisitorBuilder` and `WalkParallel::visit` let external code supply per-thread visitors with owned state, as an alternative to the closure-based `run`.
`WalkBuilder::filter_entry` and `add_custom_ignore_filename` are the per-caller filtering hooks; ripgrep itself uses the latter to register `.rgignore`.

agent_handoff.summary: Read `crates/core/main.rs`, `crates/core/flags/mod.rs` and `crates/core/flags/hiargs.rs` first — they define the whole control flow and the low→high argument split that every other decision hangs off. Formatting is enforced (`rustfmt.toml`: `max_width = 79`, `use_small_heuristics = "max"`, edition 2024) and CI fails on `cargo fmt --all --check`, so run rustfmt before proposing a diff. Most changes that touch the CLI require edits in three coordinated places: the `Flag` impl, the `FLAGS` slice, and the corresponding `LowArgs`/`HiArgs` fields. Note the repository's `AI_POLICY.md`: autonomous agents are explicitly barred from contributing upstream, and AI-written comments to maintainers may be hidden — treat this repo as read/analyze-friendly but do not open PRs or issues on it autonomously.

claims.claim: `AI_POLICY.md` states "Autonomous agents are not allowed to be used for contributing to this project" and that PRs appearing in violation will be closed, possibly without notice; `CONTRIBUTING.md` says contributions not following it will be closed.

Read first, in order: `crates/core/main.rs` (dispatch), `crates/core/flags/mod.rs` (the `Flag` trait and `Category`), `crates/core/flags/hiargs.rs` (`from_low_args` and every builder accessor), `crates/core/search.rs` (`SearchWorker`).

The core crate's own README warns it is not a library and is "glue code that brings the grep-matcher, grep-regex, grep-searcher and grep-printer crates together" — behavior changes usually belong in a `crates/*` library, not in core.
Formatting convention is strict and narrow: `max_width = 79`, `use_small_heuristics = "max"`, `edition = "2024"`; the `rustfmt` CI job runs `cargo fmt --all --check`.

Adding a flag requires: a unit struct implementing `Flag` (with `doc_long` in mdoc format), an entry in `FLAGS` at the right position for doc ordering, a field in `LowArgs`, and usually a matching field/accessor in `HiArgs`.

Per-flag tests use `parse_low_raw([...])`, a `#[cfg(test)]`-only helper that runs the parser once with no logging and no config file — the right tool for asserting flag parsing without touching the environment.
By convention `Flag::update` must only validate, never act: the trait docs use `--hostname-bin` as the example of work that must be deferred so it happens once, later.

Tests to run: `cargo test --all` for the full suite, `cargo test --features pcre2` to double-run integration tests under PCRE2, `cargo test --workspace --features unstable-index` for index tests, and `ci/test-complete` for zsh completions.

Integration tests create real files in a temp dir and run the built `rg` binary — they are not hermetic against the host, and `cmd_exists` gating means missing `gzip`/`xz` silently reduces coverage rather than failing.

Trap: `Flag::name_long` must be ≥2 ASCII alphanumeric/`-` characters and short flags must be unique ASCII alphanumeric or `.`; violating either fails `longs_all_ascii_alphanumeric`/`shorts_no_duplicates` rather than failing to compile.

Trap: changing thread-count derivation can trip `assert_eq!(1, self.threads, "sorting implies single threaded")` in `walk_builder`, because `--sort` and parallelism are mutually exclusive by construction.

Trap: in parallel mode the printer must not own the file separator — `printer_standard` only calls `separator_search` when `self.threads == 1`, because the `BufferWriter` owns separator logic otherwise.
